utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. I can follow the proceedings in my mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Oric. You may sit down, and good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Patricia Sellers from the Office of the Prosecutor. With me today is co-counsel, Mr. Gramsci di Fazio, Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our case manager Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink. And good morning to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you Ms. Sellers, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends from the OTP. My name is Vasvija Vidovic and together with Mr. John Jones I appear for Naser Oric. With us are our legal assistants, Ms. Adisa Mehic and Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Vidovic and good morning to you and your team. So any preliminaries? Okay. So I give the floor again to Madam Vidovic and afterwards to Mr. Jones. We'll have a break at 10.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yesterday I concluded with a part in which I dealt with communications. And this is where I will continue. In the OTP's reply to our final brief in footnote 253 of paragraph 128, they invoked several documents claiming that Oric forwarded the information mentioned in those documents to his superiors. Your Honours, please take a look at those documents. Those are no standardised military reports. Those are reports on the situation in the field as well as requests for assistance. The condition of communications in Srebrenica was best described by their own witness, Mr. Ibrahim Becirovic in his testimony of the 26th of April 2005, on pages 7708 and 7709 of the transcript. I wanted to quote a small portion of his testimony. His answer: "In my testimony so far, I've been trying to explain that to my knowledge, there were no means of communication used by something I wouldn't even call the staff of the armed forces. I spoke about these poorly organised groups in the area of Srebrenica." Question: "All right. I will ask you something else, then. This document confirms, does it not, that those people went in action with no means of communication whatsoever? Answer: You are right." Apart from this statement by one of the OTP's witnesses, from which one can clearly see that the staff possessed no means of communication, still the OTP claimed that there was such a thing as communications department headed by Hamed Alic. Irrespective of Mr. Becirovic who was their witness on the 20th of April 2005 on page 744 of the transcript, said that the information and communications service headed by Hamed Alic formed part of the War Presidency and in spite of him saying that on the 21st of April 2005 on page 7523 of the transcript, he said that the messages sent to Sarajevo and Tuzla were actually sent on behalf of the War Presidency of Srebrenica. He clearly explained that he usually himself received such information speaking with the refugees and the wounded. He said that his information as regards the situation in the field was not received from the fighters. Another Prosecution [as interpreted] witness, Lieutenant Colonel Rex Dudley in his testimony on the 14th of December 2005, on page 15024 of the transcript explained -- Your Honours, I said Defence witness, Lieutenant Colonel Rex Dudley instead of Prosecution witness. In his testimony on the 14th of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... will try to adopt him.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He explained, "As I said earlier, C3I, that is command/control/communications and intelligence, altogether form vital parts of a good, effective command and control for any commander in the field. If you are missing one or several of these components, you won't be able to effectively control your command." Could we see slide 30, please, now? Slide 30, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is on screen. Do you have a problem with your monitor? Do you press the right button? The one on the left in the middle?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is all right now. Thank you, Your Honour. In another part of his testimony on the 13th of December 2005, on page 14905, Lieutenant Colonel Rex Dudley stated the following: Question: "And I want to take it -- well, first of all based on your observations, did the conditions exist for a commander to be effective on the ground?" Answer: "In the situation in Srebrenica, I don't think any commander who walked into that environment would be very successful." Question: "And do you make that observation in terms as well of the training, equipment, and conditions necessary to organise military operations into planned, sustained operations?" Answer: "Yes. Not only was the equipment missing, but a key component, communications, was also missing from that enclave." Question: "Now, how important are good communications to command and control?" Answer: "Very. Particularly for more complex combat operations. I would like to make a point here that the terrain of Srebrenica was very broken up, very hilly, very compartmentalised, and therefore, being able to communicate with subordinate leaders or commanders on the ground, you would have to have good, solid communications between a commander, subordinate commanders, to make sure that the forces stay coordinated in a well-involved complex plan that people knew so that they would deal with various contingencies they would run into in their area of operation." Your Honours, effective command, therefore, first and foremost, demands good communication between the commander and his subordinates, between the commander and his superiors, as well as in between units and formations. It doesn't suffice, as the Prosecutor stated, that there was this possibility of communication. That possibility in the conditions of Srebrenica and its besieged villages was at its most primitive level, that pertained to the most basic contacts as regards danger and assistance requests. A military commander should have standing communication with his subordinates, and his subordinates in turn should have good communication with, say, their subordinates, company commanders, and they in turn with their subordinate platoon commanders and so on and so forth. This is how one sets up the layers of an organisation. A commander at a lower level should communicate with his subordinates and control them and then report to his superior as to the position and activities, the situation with ammunition and reserves, as well as enemy activities. A commander, in order to have effective control, needs to have a clear, precise, and realistic picture of everything taking place within his area of responsibility when it comes to both his and enemy forces. What is important to stress is that for him to have that image in his head, he needs to be able to do that without visiting every single subordinate unit on the ground and possibly without direct communication via radio. A commander, in order to achieve effective control, needs to have the preconditions to prepare and issue clear and concise orders in standardised format, that his trained subordinates could understand and carry out. On the other land, lower-ranking commanders have to submit regular reports on the situation, also in a standardised format so that their superior commander would at any given time have full information. In order to command, a commander has to have trained staff to prepare and analyse reports and to coordinate information. In order to command, he has to have lower-ranking officers, that is mid-level officers, they have to have rank, they have to have radio connection and monitor them. A commander would have to have such staff to be able to be sure that all the information he receives is forwarded to appropriate instances and organised. Therefore it is of crucial importance to use a standardised system of reporting. This concerns all military activity, requests for food, water, urgent requests to evacuate victims, as well as requests for various logistics issues, and all other military issues, since we are talking about a military commander. It is of crucial importance to have a timely and efficient transmission of information as regards all issues important for military activities. A timely and efficient transmission yet again demands training of staff as regards reporting. Without trained staff the commander can only scream and hope for the best. A communication network does not serve only to transmit orders but also to secure the flow of information. Without such information, commanding is simply impossible. In brief, to carry out effective control, one needs to have the command infrastructure, including communications, information, trained staff, standardised reporting, and an intelligence service. There are neither adequate means of communication, nor a standard infrastructure to prepare and issue military orders and to forward information in the form of various reports, no control is possible, let alone an effective one. Your Honours, was there any command infrastructure in Srebrenica? No, there wasn't. Can we call this so-called staff of the armed forces an organised military command? No. Because they lacked the basic preconditions: No logistics, no trained staff, no means of communication, no preconditions for standardised reporting, and no means to timely and efficiently convey information. There were no trained subordinates and it did not have troops who underwent the -- even basic treatment -- training. The soldiers in Srebrenica were young and a lot of them were not even adults and they did not undergo the basic JNA training. Even in the so-called staff -- Your Honours, again there is an error. I'm getting English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. This has now been corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not even in the so-called staff did Oric exercise command. In the staff itself, Oric was not in command. According to the war diary, P84, extensively used by the Prosecutor, for example, on pages in the original 02115054, 02115066, 02115079, 02115089, and many others, it says that they sat down and discussed among themselves and voted, they being the local leaders. Mirsad, Ahmo, Zulfo, Nedzad. They talked about their men. They said, "My men need this. My men have done that." Very often, they did this together with the members of the War Presidency. They voted. Oric's vote was not worth more than anybody else's. Is this command, Your Honours? No. Are these the powers of a commander? No. This is decision-making, equivalent to decision-making in a local commune. When discussing issues of interest for the local areas. People sit down and they vote according to the principle of representation. Once again, this is not command. In order to prove that Oric was the Supreme Commander of the area, they showed video P427 where Naser is seen talking with UN soldiers. The suggestion was that this was a meeting with Philippe Morillon but we didn't see him on the video. However that may be, Your Honours, I'm convinced that you have observed that precisely in that part of the footage that was shown, Oric said, "I cannot issue orders to the people. I will not raise weapons against my own people." He said this at 00:49:23. And now, please let us see slide 31. Your Honours, take a brief look at part of this same video, P427, the time is 00:45:50 to 00:46:52. What the Prosecutor did not tell you is that in that same place, at that same time, the same UN soldiers were also talking to the commander of Cerska, Semso Salihovic. The transcript of this part of the footage is our Exhibit D826 and I quote from part of this conversation, Semso Salihovic: "Does the world know that these people are suffocating? Does the world know -- listen, the world knows what it's doing in order to suffocate Islam in this area. They are sending ut Philippe Morillon, a real Chetnik. Is there any justice? But the world has turned towards us in order to destroy us, you see. They put Philippe Morillon at the head, who is doing the job assigned to him by the world. How powerful that world is. He knows that these people have been fighting for a year and what has the people been fighting with? 30.000 people, with little rifles. Do you know how many men I lost to get this rifle? No more or less than ten fighters for this rifle." These are the words by -- spoken by him on this video.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honours, you have also seen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just a question. With whom did Semso Salihovic talk here? Who was the man on the tank? With whom did he talk?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, the UN military --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, he was talking to the same people to whom Naser Oric was speaking on the footage shown yesterday. This part of the footage is only two minutes before the part shown by the Prosecutor yesterday. So it's part of the same video, Oric and Semso Salihovic are both talking to a group of UN representatives, not including Morillon. Morillon was not seen on the part of the footage played by the Prosecutor either. You have also seen, from another video that we played during the testimony of Mr. Ejub Guster, that Mr. Morillon also spoke to others, for example Mr. Talovic. Therefore, the part of the video which they showed, showing Oric talking to UN soldiers, does not prove what they want it to prove; that is, that Oric showed that he had the authority of Supreme Commander because he spoke to the UN. As you have been able to see all local leaders spoke to the UN, and you have been able to see the commander of Cerska, Semso Salihovic, doing the same. What kind of control, de facto, did Oric have over the groups in the eastern enclaves? This is illustrated by footage of a session of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina held on the 11th of August 1995, and this is D300. Your Honours, you have here part of document D300, where General Rasim Delic, the Commander of the Main Staff of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1995, August 1995, after the fall of Srebrenica, was certainly in a position to have information about the Muslim forces in Srebrenica during the war. And this is what he said. In the discussion -- the part of the discussion that has to do with Oric's role. I quote, "However, my information, now that he has come here and that the army has come, is that he did not have much influence except on his brigade. He was not the kind of commander who had command over the situation in the division. He had command over his own brigade and another one. He had no influence over the others. "So the level of military organisation in that area was low. We tried to bring as much influence as bear as we could in writing by orders and summoning all commanders. Unfortunately it did not work."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic, the second line on the script that we have here does not correspond with what the interpreter said when she was translating, interpreting, what were you saying in your own language. Here it says, "He did not have much influence on his brigade as commander." What the interpreter told us is that he did not have much influence except on his brigade. The two are quite different. So perhaps you can repeat again in your own language what is at your disposal and then the interpreters will have a second opportunity to interpret to us so that at least we have a clear indication of which one of the two versions is the correct one. It's the first two lines that you have to read.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I now have the original transcript in Bosnian, of that session and it says, "However, my information now, now that he has come here, and now that the army has come here, is he did not have some command influence on his brigade." I agree that it's a little confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is exactly the -- not exactly the opposite but it's completely different from what we have written down in D300.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just to clarify, what brigade is he talking about and at -- what time frame did Delic have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Delic is referring to the situation after the fall of Srebrenica in 1995, and he says that the level of military organisation in that area was low, even in 1995. He refers to the brigade Oric originated from. It's not very clear from what he said, but Your Honours know what evidence Oric -- what brigade Oric originated from. I will clarify this. Your Honours, we believe that the translation in D300 corresponds to the original but to clarify I will say the following: Rasim Delic said this referring to the organisation of the Muslim forces in 1995 in that area, which was very low. Your Honours, imagine, then, what this organisation looked like in 1992 and 1993. This organisation must have been even poorer, at an even lower level, and many witnesses have spoken about this, both Prosecution and Defence witnesses, and now, Your Honours, I will refer to another aspect. Naser Oric, as a commander, in 1992, was 25 years old. He had completed a police course, had done his regular military service in the JNA, and he had no training in command. Your Honours, even the most gifted, charismatic, and brilliant military leader must be trained to be a commander. This training includes various skills that a commander must have in order to, to say the very least, understand what his subordinates are able to do and what they are not able to do. He had to have gone through such training to know what he can realistically expect from his subordinates in the given circumstances. He had to have gone through training in order to know how to compose and issue an order, how to understand intelligence information, how to lead his key staff properly. The sensitivity required by command is not easily acquired. Military training in various schools and military academies is aimed at training people to be good tacticians and good operative commanders. What I wish to say, Your Honours, is that you cannot expect effective military command to be established by chance, without the proper training or preparation. A commander, therefore, needs careful training and education. Naser Oric did not have this. For someone to command, he needs to have accumulated military experience. Naser Oric did not have it. Neither did his subordinates. He did not go through any kind of training in international humanitarian law, never, neither he nor his subordinates. The legislation in this area was not available to him so that he could train himself or train his subordinates. Never was this delivered to Srebrenica. Your Honours, when issuing your judgement, you will certainly bear these facts in mind. Your Honours, you will now be addressed by my colleague. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic. Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. May it please Your Honours I'll be dealing with questions of documentary evidence, the law, the detention charges and finally sentencing. Now, Your Honours, the Prosecution says that its case against Naser Oric is based primarily on circumstantial evidence, which it picturesquely compares to chain mail armour and it says this in its final brief in paragraph 8, "The circumstantial evidence presented in this case is not like a single chain whereby when one link fails, the entire chain breaks. Rather it is like chain mail armour, the links are intertwined in such a way that when one link fails, the armour's strength is not diminished." Now, this is an interesting metaphor. First, one wonders why the Prosecution needs to use a metaphor to explain what happens when links in the chain of circumstantial evidence fail. It's a tacit admission, is it not, that many links, many items of evidence, do not in fact support the Prosecution's case. Just how many links have failed will be for Your Honours to judge. We've made our position very clear in our closing brief, in our response to the Prosecution brief, and in my colleague's closing speech. The case has failed completely. The chain mail metaphor is based on a notion of mutually corroborating evidence, in particular exhibits. On Monday Mr. Di Fazio gave some examples to support his claim of mutual corroboration. Recall, however, that what stands together must also fall together. Mutual support also means mutual collapse. Mr. Di Fazio referred to P80 and P570 as being mutually supporting, since they both give the same exact number of recruits the TO Osmace, A3, namely 121 and the same applies to P571 allegedly the members of TO Biljeg, 136 members. But remember what witnesses said about P80. Hakija Meholjic, a Prosecution witness, condemned P80 in the strongest possible terms. He said, "This document has nothing whatsoever to do with the reality of the situation at the time." Is there any more forceful way of condemning a document as untrue? I don't believe so. So what does that say about P80 mutually supporting P570 and P571? Well, it follows if P80 has nothing to do with the reality on the ground, then P570 and P571 are equally suspect. If they stand together then they fall together too. So with the links in the Prosecution's chain mail armour, if one fails the others do not necessarily hold firm. They may unravel for the same reason. Your Honours, as a child I saw many specimens of chain mail armour in the Tower of London and other places. It's usually displayed in some disembodied form, hanging from a wall or draped over a dummy. Much as in this case the chain mail doesn't rest on anything substantial, anything living, any real. It's draped over a shell, an empty form. Just as the Prosecution's case is draped over the empty shelf its own theorising. Witnesses who could confirm the Prosecution's theory of a unified command in Srebrenica, among other things, are what are conspicuously missing from this case. Your Honours may have heard of the Sherlock Holmes story, the adventure of silver blades, in which this exchange took place, Inspector Gregory says, "Is there any other points to which you it would wish to draw my attention?" Holmes: "To the curious incidents of the dog in the night-time." Gregory: "The dog did nothing in the night-time." Holmes: "That was the curious incident. The curious incident is that the guard dog did not bark, as one would have expected, which signalled that the dog knew the intruder." If what the Prosecution said about the situation in Srebrenica were true, that the accused was at the apex of a unified command, that the documents on which the Prosecution seeks to rely may be relied upon, then there would have been a barking dog, a witness from Srebrenica, who would have appeared before you and said, "Yes, that was the situation. Yes. These documents do reflect the reality on the ground." They never did, the dog never barked, and that's what is curious about this case. In a criminal trial, Your Honour, there are cumulative elements, many cumulative elements, that have to be proved beyond a reasonable doubt. Each and every one has to be proved and if one fails, the whole case fails. And a bold Prosecutor will admit as much that their case depends on those links holding firm. But not our Prosecutor. They seek refuge in a metaphor which is only appropriate inasmuch as it evokes images of a disintegrating and disembodied fabric. Your Honour, there is a better metaphor for the Prosecution's case and it's circumstantial evidence, it's a patch work immediate from many different clots. You can think of each item of evidence as a different colour clot. And with a snip here and a snip there, selecting different parts of different materials, different parts of different documents, the Prosecution might be able to put together an untidy mosaic. You would have to ignore the pile of discarded fabric to fool yourself into thinking that this mosaic was the complete picture. You would have to ignore that huge pile of discarded material to conclude that the Prosecution has proved any of the counts beyond a reasonable doubt. Now, P50 provides a good example of this, but there are hundreds of such examples. And we can call P50 up on to the monitor. The Prosecution relies on P50 to show that a victim named in the indictment, Milisav Milovanovic died. But they dispute the cause of death as stated in that document, namely pneumonia. So you would have to use just part of this document and ignore the rest. You would have to take a pair of scissors, figuratively speaking, and cut out the bit that the Prosecution needs for its case and then throw the rest in the bin. Or P84, the war diary or P561 the diary found in a meadow. The Prosecution would invite you to look at anything which seems to link the military police with the staff but to ignore anything and everything that shows that the military police came under the command of the War Presidency. The scissors of injustice would have to again be applied to cut away anything exculpatory. When it comes to the detention charges, the Prosecution would ignore, as they did in their speech on Tuesday, what Mr. Zikic said referring to Beli, never referring to Kemo in the SUP, referring to people being beaten outside the SUP, not inside the SUP on the day of the exchange, and not mentioning any incident when Sarac was allegedly slapped by the accused. But then they would then turn around and ask to you rely on Zikic that the detainees had visible signs of injury, and ignore what Radic said on the subject, namely that there were no visible signs of injury on them. And they would ask to you simply gloss over all their problems with the alleged identification of the accused in the SUP and the building. And they would ask you to forget that Ejub Guster ever testified about a black Mercedes that remained in the same place on the day of C-007's exchange and about Morillon and Oric not being present at that exchange. Well, Your Honours, I invite the Trial Chamber to infer that whenever the Prosecution has ignored or glossed over important exculpatory evidence, that it's because they have no answer to that evidence. And you will draw the appropriate conclusions from that. In order to find the accused guilty of any of the charges in the indictment you would also have to take the scissors of injustice to cut up the transcripts of the evidence of most of the Prosecution witnesses. Dr. Mujkanovic, Hakija Meholjic, Ibro Becirovic, Colonel Tucker, Judge Omerovic, Dr. Gow, as well as large parts of the testimony of Brkic, Hogic, and Delic. You'd have to practically shred those transcripts and place all that exculpatory evidence in a dustbin too. Mr. Di Fazio tried to pretend on Tuesday that only Dr. Mujkanovic's evidence runs directly counter to their case. Not so. It's true of all of the Prosecution witnesses that I've just mentioned. Now, on the subject of asking the Trial Chamber to disbelieve its own witness, I can probably do no better than to quote what Your Honour said at the start of the Brdjanin trial. It was the hearing of 24 January 2002, page 805, and Your Honour said this: "Well, the system that this Trial Chamber opts for is that if you bring forward a witness you're expecting not to attack the credibility of that witness." In other words, we are talking of your witness and therefore you're expected to bring forward witnesses that you have consulted with beforehand that more or less you know what kind of evidence they are going to produce. Now if that witness at any point in time in the course of the testimony turns against you, and disrupts what you had planned to get from that particular witness, him or her being your witness, then obviously you're going to be faced with a difficult situation. And it may well be you would prefer to bring forward previous statements made by that witness that are contradictory to what that witness would be stating during these proceedings. This is what I'm referring to. You will not be allowed to contradict the witness until you first obtain permission of the Trial Chamber to do so. In other words," I'm still quoting Your Honour." In other words, once you have taken the position to produce that witness as your witness in support of that case the practice will be that you do not try to discredit that witness." Then on page 806, "So the rule is that once you have close tonne bring forward a witness, it's because you believe in the credibility of that witness." "So the rule is that once you've chosen to bring forward a witness it's because you believe in the credibility of that witness." Now what Your Honour said was also stated in Limaj in an oral decision of 1st of February 2005 "the general position is that a party calling a witness may not discredit that witness." So indeed there is ample authority at this Tribunal for that proposition. The Prosecution has not applied to treat any of its witnesses as hostile. Not Mujkanovic, not Mehojlic, not Ibro Becirevic, not one of them, and that means that to this day they believe in the credibility of all those witnesses. Now, they cannot now invite Your Honours to find those witnesses not credible. They are stuck with that evidence. And they know that. So they don't explicitly ask you to disbelieve those witnesses. No, they do it covertly, implicitly. The Prosecution tries to suggest to you with a nod and a wink, and if you're in any doubt that's what Mr. Di Fazio was doing on Tuesday, with a nod and a wink saying, "Disbelieve Mujkanovic, even though he was our witness," and it's what he did when he put to Colonel Tucker that Dr. Mujkanovic was just a loiterer outside the hospital and not what he really was, a hero who had done a great number of incredibly important operations in the hospital. No, with a hint, he said you should not believe Dr. Mujkanovic, their own witness whom they proofed and then presented to you as a witness of truth. Well, Your Honours, I have to say what an irresponsible attitude that is to try and shift the burden on to you. It's their case which they have to prove beyond a reasonable doubt. And Your Honours will be perfectly entitled to say for any point in contention, this was evidence brought by you, the Prosecution, which you did not seek to challenge when it was given by your witness, and that therefore you have failed to discharge your burden of proof on that matter. Equally it apply us for us. We are entitled to rely on the fact that evidence has been given by a Prosecution witness, that they haven't sought to challenge that witness, and we are perfectly entitled to consider, "Well, we don't need to call evidence on that point because their own witness has said it and not been challenged." Your Honours, it's as if I were to provide a recommendation to you for, let's say a cleaning person, and after they started work I were then to inform you that you should be careful because they might start pocketing your finer silver. What would you think of me if I did that? But that's what the Prosecution is doing with regard to Dr. Mujkanovic. I would ask what sort of a world is the Prosecution living in if they think that's a proper approach to a criminal trial? How does the Prosecution dare to hint or to suggest to you that maybe you should disbelieve some of their witnesses which it called to give evidence before you, under oath, and whom they never sought to impeach? If the Prosecution at any time was surprised by the evidence of any of their witnesses, surprised in light of their proofing, their preparation of their witness, such as to cause them to believe that the witnesses might not be telling the truth to your Trial Chamber, on oath, then they had a duty, an absolute professional duty, at that moment to apply to impeach that witness and they never did. So that means the Prosecution believe in and vouch for the credibility of every single witness they called. Unlike the Prosecution, we stand by our witnesses, all of them. We wouldn't dream of surreptitiously asking Your Honours to disbelieve what any of our witnesses told you under oath. We stand by them, and by the testimony that they gave. And any other approach would completely undermine the whole notion of a criminal trial. You may get a further sense of the world inhabited by our prosecutors when you hear their repeated references to an alleged conspiracy theory. Aware that their documents have not been confirmed by witnesses and following the maxim that the best defence is offence, the Prosecution seeks to ridicule any challenge to the authenticity or even the validity of its documents as being the product of a conspiracy theory. They even go so far as to say that the positing of conspiracy theory is a central plank in the Defence case. As Your Honours are well aware we never alleged some huge conspiracy. That cliched phrase is of the Prosecution's own invention. Yes, we say that some signatures have been forged. Other documents might have been put together years after events so that, as witnesses like Meholjic confirmed they don't reflect the situation on the ground at the time and that others contain palpably false information. It's not for us to provide some grand, unified theory of why Prosecution exhibits cannot be relied upon. They have the burden of proving that their documents may be relied upon. And as Your Honour stated in your guidelines on evidence issued at the start of this case on the 21st of October 2004, "the Trial Chamber will follow the principal that the Prosecution must prove relevance, probative value, and reliability of such evidence beyond a reasonable doubt." Now, the Prosecution has a heavy burden to discharge in order to satisfy Your Honour that is its exhibits are relevant, probative and reliable. The Prosecution calls in aid the notion of a conspiracy theory in order to try to shrug off that burden of proof. Or even to try to put the burden of proof on to us. But we don't need to advance any theory as to why the Prosecution's exhibits are unreliable. We simply point out the facts. Take, for example, P19, an exhibit stating that Pejic is dead when he's alive. I don't know why the document says that. I do know that it's unreliable for that reason. And when we consider that certain documents are not reliable, we are not alone in this. Your Honours have excluded two exhibits, P65 and P68 based on our objections to authenticity, and the Prosecution too evidently finds something fishy about certain of its own exhibits. Prosecution Exhibit P50 which we looked at a moment ago, in which the Prosecution disputes the cause of death as stated in that document. Now, I presume the Prosecution are not challenging the medical expertise of Dr. Hasanovic. They say that Milisav Milovanovic was beaten to death. Whereas that document states that there were no signs of injury. No, the Prosecution is saying there is something not right about P50, something fraudulent, maybe even some sort of a cover-up. Do we label that as a conspiracy theory in order to dismiss it? No. We say that's a legitimate submission - legitimate, I say, not necessarily valid - but that a certain document has suspects features and it's to that extent unreliable. Dr. Kerzan, the Trial Chamber's own expert didn't see anything extraordinary in the suggestion that a Prosecution exhibit might bear a forged signature of the accused. On the contrary, he testified that there was a "quite strong possibility" that the signature on P14 was "a falsified signature." Did Dr. Kerzan suddenly taken leave of his senses and become infected by the Defence's wild conspiracy theory? No. He was recognising what is in fact a pretty mundane occurrence, namely the possibility that someone has copied someone else's signature. It happens every day. On the subject of Dr. Kerzan, yes, I suggested that his approach might be coloured by subjectivity as a policeman, as a police expert, someone who works in a police laboratory and whose previous work at the ICTY has only been for the Prosecution. I suggest that he had a tendency, perhaps even unconscious, to downplay the possibility that the alleged signature of the accused was not in fact his. I have great respect for Dr. Kerzan who gave careful and considered evidence, although he worked, as he himself admitted, in a bit of a hurry. But it's not a conspiracy theory to suggest that he has unconscious tendencies to exaggerate or to downplay certain features. And incidently he too gave absolute conclusions on documents, it was not only Professor Bilic who did so. It was the Prosecution's expert, Dr. Fagel he will who was in a minority in never committing fully to a conclusion. And on the subject of Professor Bilic, in my submission he had in fact the best range and variety of non-contentious signatures of the accused that they dated from 1996, 1999, 2001, and 2003, and were produced for different purposes which the literature recognises as the best sample. Again in the context of the conspiracy theory, the Prosecution referred to the Dutch video, "The Uncrowned King of Srebrenica." But we suggest that the title of the video itself shows bias. It's a stupid title, to be honest, and you can see right away where the makers of that film are headed when you see the title. And even more so when you see the crudely edited content. Now, of course, there are films and documentaries which are polemical biased, sensationalist, or otherwise unprofessional. I don't know why this film was made and I don't know why the Dutch Evangelical Church saw fit to give a copy of the video to the Prosecution. As I say that's a matter for them. It's not for us to provide an all encompassing explanation for these things. As my colleague mentioned yesterday, the Prosecution knows full well that it's relying on documents which bear major indicia of unreliability. They took witness statements from several witnesses, Dr. Hasanovic, Dr. Pilav, Djanan Djananovic [phoen], Radomir Hodzic [phoen], who said that they did not sign documents purportedly signed by them or who otherwise cast doubt on the authenticity of documents shown to them by the Prosecution. Some of these people were originally on the Prosecution's witness list. The Prosecution simply dropped them and then continued to rely on the documents any way as exhibits. Now, Your Honours, the Prosecution cannot honestly ask you to believe that no one's signature is ever forged and that every signature and every document is exactly what it purports to be. You have to look into these matters. I would add, Your Honour, a matter which is referred to in our final -- in our closing brief and in the response, there is the confusion, the constant confusion, between form and content, that even once one establishes the document is authentic, that says nothing about whether the contents of the document are true or not. That's an entirely separate question. Now at the opening of the trial the Prosecution said that raising these issues of authenticity was a smoke screen and now they've stumbled on a new term, conspiracy theory. They seem to be fond of terms from Hollywood. We heard of the Wild Bunch conspiracy theory in Madonna in only two days of the Prosecution's closing arguments. It's a very old tactic to seek to discredit your opponent's position by first representing it and then ridiculing the misrepresented position rather than addressing the true position. And that's what they've done here. I know Your Honours will not be impressed by that tactic Moreover, the Prosecution's position on documents betrays a complete double standard. The Prosecution received many documents in this case from the Republika Srpska bureau for cooperation with the ICTY and through Dejan Miletic who was fired by the High Representative for, among other things, document concealment. In Blagojevic the Prosecution stated that the RS government "sets out to perpetuate myths and lies." Myths and lies. And that was in relation to the genocide in Srebrenica. And in that case the Prosecution stated that the RS published "gross propaganda." Gross propaganda and precisely in relation to Srebrenica and that the RS "cannot be relied upon in any serious matter." Any serious matter. Well, this trial is a serious matter, I hope, so if the Prosecution were true too its towards, they would not rely on organs of the RS and certainly not to the huge extent that had has done in this case. Most honourable people are held to their words and I wouldn't expect the Prosecution to be any less honourable. Those are its own words, the RS perpetuates myths and lies. The RS publishes gross propaganda, and the RS cannot be relied upon in any serious matter. Now, if the Prosecution meant those strong words and I have no doubt that they meant them entirely when they said them in Blagojevic then what should -- so that should give them pause about accepting wholesale whatever exhibits the RS or Bosnian Serbs deliver to them in this case against their erstwhile enemy. Remember that the Prosecution's exhibits are not all seized collections. Many of them were provided individually by RS organs or state officials in response to requests nor assistance or RFAs from the Prosecution. And the exhibits in which the Prosecution most relies in this case, P598, P590, P608, for example, are precisely those with no chain of custody which have not even been introduced by a Prosecution investigator, and which have been authenticated by no one. Exhibits such as a diary found in a meadow, undated lists from who knows where and created who knows when, photocopies of alleged diaries but without the author being called to testify about the entries. As far as the Republika Srpska as a source is concerned, if I'd been sold a dud car by a used car salesman I wouldn't go back there at all. If I had to go back, I would be very, very careful before accepting what that salesman told me about his used cars. And to use a Biblical metaphor if I had to dine with that person I would take with me a very long spoon. But as we warned in our opening speech, black is white in this case and white is black, and so here we are told in so many words that the RS government is a trustworthy and honourable source, and any document provided by the RS can be relied upon fully even without chain of custody evidence, and even without any witness confirming the truth of the document's content. That is yet another myth by the Prosecution. On the subject of chain of custody, Mr. Di Fazio said on Monday that because archives from Srebrenica were seized by the Serbs there would never be a complete chain of custody back to the source. That may be true for some documents, not for all, mind, but that does not explain why there was no chain of custody evidence once those documents were in Serb hands. Why, as Radijevic [phoen] testified, Odivecic [phoen], excuse me, documents were apparently dumped in someone's safe for years on end rather than being properly logged and archived in accordance with the strict practice tan rules of the Drina Corps. Now, two final words on documents. The Prosecution says that our approach to documents is selective because we have also used documents from Serb sources, including the Sokolac collection. Well, as Your Honours are well aware, we have used documents from that collection as exhibits precisely to illustrate the documents from the Sokolac collection are inherently unreliable, and we introduced 17 documents from the Sokolac collection, and 12 of them we used to make our point about the lack of authenticity of documents, and five documents showing lists of killed persons which we also found in the Drina Corps collection were used because we had independent indicia of their reliability. And I have the exhibit numbers if Your Honour needs them. The Prosecution does not seem to understand or not want to understand that exhibits are tendered for different purposes. They argued that we relied on prior statements of witnesses because we tendered them into evidence. For example the prior witness statement of Mr. Zikic. However, as I'm sure Your Honours understood we tendered prior statements of Prosecution witnesses to impeach those witnesses by showing prior contradictions, not to rely on those statements as to proof of the truth of their contents. There was also, Your Honours a fundamental distinction between documents of the Drina Corps and Bratunac Brigade on which were seized by the OTP at source, on the one hand, and then documents allegedly captured by the Serbs from the enemy and then delivered to the OTP by the Serbs. There is an obvious difference in reliability in terms of those two categories. And finally on documents, Your Honour, I would like to respond to the Prosecution's remarks on Monday that by setting out our position regarding documents for which there was no chain of custody and about which no witnesses commented. We don't propose any iron-clad rule that documents not shown to witnesses or which have no chain of custody evidence are per se inadmissible or of no probative value --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you proceed on this, let me make myself clear because on Monday I did hint that you both have tendered documents which you then did not use with your witnesses. The essential difference between Prosecution and the Defence is the following: That to my knowledge, out of the 315 documents that you did not use with your witnesses, in your final brief you only referred to two, and it's a neutral use of those two documents. In the case of the Prosecution, out of the number of documents that you did not put to your witnesses, quite a few of them that you rely specifically rely upon in your final brief and in your response. This is the difference between the Prosecution and the Defence. And this is what I would like you to address in your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. That was indeed one of the points I was going to make. I believe it's, with one exception, I think it's D513, we don't place reliance on any of the exhibits which -- or any of our own exhibits which have not been shown to witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You refer only, I think, to D454 and 513. Again, I am specifically saying that one is a decision proclaiming state of war in the Serb Autonomous Region of Birac and the other one is a declaration of threat of war from the Presidency of the Serbian Republic. So these are not exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The situation of the Prosecution use of such documents is somewhat different so ... I don't have the list. I have it here but it's somewhere. But any way, let's proceed. I don't want to take any of your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour did anticipate precisely what I was going to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 198 out of 625, there are 198 documents that you did not put to witnesses, and I have myself then marked all the ones that you have basically referred to in your final brief and in your response and there were quite a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, and for the record that's Prosecution documents, just so it's clear on the record. 198 which have not been put to witnesses. For our part, we do not place reliance on exhibits which were not shown to witnesses in our closing brief. As Your Honour has noted, those two exceptions are extracts from the Official Gazette of the Serbian people whose existence may be independently verified in the Official Gazette, and so that's a separate category. A second the Prosecution has not challenged the authenticity of our exhibits whereas we have challenged the authenticity of many of their exhibits, and that too is a very important difference. If we introduce an exhibit and the Prosecution does not challenge its authenticity, then in our submission there is no harm in it remaining in the record for Your Honours to consider just as admitted facts and stipulations may substitute for evidence a document has to which there is no dispute may, of course, be considered by the Trial Chamber. But not so with exhibits where one party --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hate to interrupt you but in my records at least or in our records, not just mine, there are still D36, D127, D725, which are a set of photos, and D822 which remain contested by the Prosecution. On one or more grounds, on different grounds basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: D36, for example, is contested on the basis of relevance but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'll review whether those documents were shown to witnesses which I imagine most of them, if not all of them, were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They definitely were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Really, it's the triple effect, if I may put it that way, Your Honour, a challenge to authenticity, the Prosecution's failure to bring evidence properly to authenticate that challenged exhibit combined with the fact that no -- that no witnesses confirmed the document's authenticity or confirmed the truth of its contents. Sorry, or challenged the failure to have any chain of custody evidence and also the fact that it hasn't been shown to a witness to comment on the contents. At that point, how can any significant probative value attach to such a document? You do not know if such a document, when it was created, by whom it was created, whether it was created by the purported author or not, why it was created, whether its contents are completely true, partially true, partially untrue, or completely false. You know nothing about the document. So to rely on such a document particularly as a Prosecution exhibit in a criminal trial of the accused is a pure leap of faith. So let me make clear that we are happy to be held to the same standard for our exhibits that we set out for Prosecution exhibits. And I would just add to that, that if the Prosecution is right in the thrust of its submission that is a paper trial can be held in which the truth of the contents of documents does not need to be established by any witness, we could have concluded this trial after Ms. Manas, the Prosecutor's investigator, introduced the exhibits at the start of the trial, we could have simply had final briefs, closing arguments, and have gone home and awaited Your Honour's verdict. It's not a serious approach on the part of the Prosecution to a criminal trial. Now, Your Honours I can turn to a consideration of the law. Will Your Honours give me one moment, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now I propose first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Jones, but I wanted to have part of the transcript copied and pasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I propose first to deal with some general legal points, then specific points in relation to command responsibility, and finally the legal issues arising in relation to the detention charges. I'll start with levee en masse. The Prosecution contests the characterisation of the forces in Srebrenica as a levee en masse. Now the standard definition of levee en masse is as set out on a slide which should appear in a moment. Yes. And that's from the third Geneva Convention, "inhabitants of a non-occupied territory who in the approach of the enemy spontaneously take up arms to resist the invading forces without having had time to form themselves to regular armed units." And then members of a levee are treated as combatants if they carry arms openly and respect the laws and customs of war. Now, consider that definition. It fits like a glove, does it not, with all the evidence that we've heard in this case of small, village-based, independent groups of fighters who traded their pitchforks for rifles in Tony Birtley's phrase, and which Hakija Meholjic also adopted at T-6961 who took up arms initially hunting rifles and then whatever they could capture from the Serbs to resist the tidal wave of the invading Serb forces who sought to and eventually did occupy the entire Drina valley. Now, Colonel Tucker who was familiar with the phrase, as a French speaker and as an extremely well-educated army officer, thought that the description of a levee en masse tallied perfectly with what he saw in Srebrenica. And that was in March 1993 just before demilitarisation. Now, the Prosecution pretends that this was a purely descriptive characterisation as if he hadn't thought through the elements. Not a bit of it. Colonel Tucker, as a high-ranking member of the British army, showed that he knew exactly what the definition of a levee en masse was when he agreed that it properly described the fighters in Srebrenica. So question: "Now, going back to the quote from your statement in Galic, civilians in the enclaves who is had taken up arms to defend themselves. The question I'm going to ask you is partly as a French speaker and as a military officer educated at Sandhurst and elsewhere, are you familiar with the expression levee en masse?" Answer: "Yes, I am." Question: "Now you told us yesterday that the Serbs had occupied 60 per cent of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the beginning of the war. So would you essentially that they were invading troops on that territory?" Answer: "On the territory that they occupied, and forced the people who were living there, usually Bosniaks, sometimes Bosnian Croats, out of the area, yes." Question: "So as a matter of military terminology, as a matter of military terminology, would you agree that Srebrenica's fighters, as far as you could tell, were a levee en masse in this sense?" Answer: Yes. Now, Colonel Tucker's description fits exactly with what Prosecution and Defence witnesses alike described. Meholjic, Mujkanovic and Becirovic, and I'm just mentioning Prosecution witnesses, all confirmed that groups of fighters throughout 1992 and up to the demilitarisation were not organised into properly formed units. Yet the Prosecution challenges this categorisation of Srebrenica's fighters as a levee en masse. Why? Well, they have to. They have to because responsibility under Article 7(3) is incompatible with a levee en masse. A levee en masse by definition is not organised under a responsible command. Now you may wonder how the Prosecution can dare to challenge the testimony of its own witnesses regarding the lack of organisation and the absence of properly formed units and uniforms amongst Srebrenica's fighters. Now, I address the question of impeaching your own witness a moment ago and this is a slightly different point: Even if the Prosecution were allowed to impeach its own witnesses by bringing forward evidence to contradict what they said, they never did so on these issues. They didn't call any evidence other than this about the state of Srebrenica's armed forces, the absence of uniforms, the absence of ranks, the lack of weapons. This is the only evidence on those subjects. So what arguments do the Prosecution seek to deploy? Well, they are not based on evidence, they are purely theoretical. The first, I suppose, is partially based on evidence. They say that Srebrenica's fighters were not a levee precisely because they were all organised under responsible command, namely the accused. Yet not a single person confirmed this. Hakija Meholjic, whose evidence the Prosecution did not challenge, testified that even after his nomination as TO commander, Naser Oric had command only over his own men "he did not have power elsewhere." Next the Prosecution argues that the fighters in Srebrenica were combatants because allegedly they had uniforms and badges. I'm quoting from paragraph 246 of the final brief. That proposition was completely refuted by the Prosecution's own witnesses. We see that on the next slide. Dr. Mujkanovic, "to speak about uniforms in Srebrenica is a futile exercise." Colonel Tucker, "no one in the Srebrenica pocket had any badges of rank that were identifiable or meaningful." Meholjic said, "there was no bread, let alone ranks, that there were no markings by which fighters could be distinguished from civilians and that anybody, civilians or fighters, could wear the ribbons or bands that were sometimes worn in actions." He said, "That there was nothing in place for efficient control." We saw that slide yesterday. Now, that's just their witnesses speaking. It's not our theory of the case. As the Prosecution suggests. It's the Prosecution's own evidence. In fact, the only people with uniforms in the area, Bosniaks, were Nurif Rizvanovic's men, and since we were not given the 400 or more documents of the Nurif Rizvanovic's collection until after the trial, the day the last witness testified we were handed these documents, in what we maintain is an appalling breach of Rule 68, probably the less said about Nurif Rizvanovic and his men the better. I simply refer to what we said about Nurif Rizvanovic in our closing brief. In its argument supposing the notion of a levee en masse the Prosecution then says if a civilian did night fight without a uniform and without a weapon, then he "becomes a war criminal" a war criminal "by feigning a civilian status." That's paragraph 245 of their closing brief and they rely on additional protocol 1's prohibition on perfidy, Article 37(1)(C) of that protocol. This is yet another extraordinary proposition by the Prosecution, that some poor soul fighting for his lifer against Serb ethnic cleansing becomes a perfidious war criminal for taking up arms against the Serbs when he doesn't have a uniform and maybe not even a weapon. And those attacking him, the Bosnian Serb army I suppose are legitimate combatants because they have nice uniforms. But we are back in Alice in Wonderland again with the Prosecution's theory of this case. In the Prosecution's hall of mirrors the Bosniak defenders of their homes are not only vicious attackers of the peace-loving Serbs in the villages surrounding them, they've now become war criminals too. That it was the, dues used by General Mladic's forces for killing 7.000 men and boys in Srebrenica in July 1995, that they were all war criminals and I shudder to think that the Prosecution's arguments in this case can now be called in aid to justify that label. Srebrenica's fighters were not war criminals but brave and desperate people fighting with tremendous courage against a superior foe. And the fact that the Prosecution prefers to argue that Srebrenica's fighters, having no uniforms, weapons or barracks, are war criminals for quote "feigning their civilian status," rather than admitting what they are, what their own witnesses said they are, a levee en masse, shows how grotesquely distorted and misguided this case has become. The Prosecution will take any position in fact or law if they think it will help to secure a conviction in this case. I ask what happened to the notion of a Prosecutor who sees his duty as being simply to present the case fairly rather than to secure a conviction at all costs? A further argument, and I think I can deal with this before the break, deployed by the Prosecution on Monday to argue against a levee en masse is as the indictment concerns attacks that's factually different from taking up arms upon the approach of the enemy but that, too, is a simplistic and misguided argument. You don't assess whether a mass of people are levee or not action by action, you can't be a levee one day and then not a levee, and then a levee again depending on whether the enemy is approaching you or you're approaching them. It's an assessment of the fighting forces as they existed in an area at a given time. I.e., is it a proper army with barracks, ranks, uniforms, armouries, salaries, and regularly formed unit or not? And by all those criteria in 1992 to 1993 Srebrenica's fighters were not a real army and time and again that was the evidence of Prosecution witnesses as well as Defence witnesses and international observers: Not a real army. The Prosecution also argues, finally, that a levee en masse can only be a temporary state of affairs because it soon gets organised. Well, that's pure theory as well. It ignores all the evidence of how things did not get better and better in Srebrenica in 1992 and 1993 but progressively worse, how villages were cut off from each other by Serb patrols, ambushes, and shelling, and how they felt that the Serb Pac-man, referring to the video game of that name, with the enemy gobbling up village by village. That's the enemy approaching. The enemy gobbling up village by village, and they were doing it in March and April of 1993 as they were in 1992. So that's another prosecutorial myth based on nothing, that things always go from good to better. In Srebrenica they went from bad to worse and finally to catastrophic. Your Honours, I think that's a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is 30 minutes good enough Mr. Jones or do you want a shorter one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm a bit concerned about the time so perhaps a shorter one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will have a 25-minute break starting now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Just two further points on levee en masse before I move on to the legal elements of murder. You will recall what Hakija Meholjic said about the use of names, even of battalions and brigades et cetera, this was simply an "arbitrary way of giving names to certain groups of people". So in regard to levee, I would ask Your Honours not to be fooled, if you like, by the fact that such names were used. Hakija Meholjic, a Prosecution witness, explained why those names were used. And secondly the Prosecution argues that Srebrenica's fighters ceased to be a levee, if it was a levee initially, on the 20th of May 1992 because of the Bajramovici meeting. Now, my colleague addressed that matter yesterday and, Your Honours, Bajramovici was a gathering of a few village leaders who decided to try to coordinate their efforts to fight the Serbs. And hundreds of villages were not involved in Bajramovici. Yet according to the Prosecution, the moment that meeting was held, somehow a cloud was lifted and the whole of the area and all the fighters became magically transformed into a proper army on that very day. Your Honours will make what you will of that suggestion. In our submission, Srebrenica was not just an example of a levee en masse, it is a paradigm example, a perfect illustration of a levee en masse in modern times of a citizenry who swapped their pitchforks for rifles to stop their lands from being occupied and from being deported or killed themselves. Now, turning to murder, I propose just to deal with the law of murder, not the evidence; that's dealt with in our brief. I would respond just to a few points, though. Firstly, regard the point raised by the Prosecution regarding causes of death. If the requirement of murder at of the perpetrator be a substantial cause of death and the evidence does amply demonstrate that the Cerska prisoners were close to death when they came to Srebrenica. And the Prosecution's arguments that the women, since the women in the prison didn't die of other cause such as pneumonia, that indicates that there was no such risk. Well, the women had not been in Cerska apart from Andja Radevic [phoen], and she wasn't beaten in Cerska, so that argument is, as I say, misplaced. The fact is a that there were many things causing death in Srebrenica in early 1993 and, we submit, Your Honours cannot simply assume that any of the prisoners who died must have been murdered. I also want to mention a couple of points in relation to the exchange of C-007. First, I find it quite incredible that the Prosecution still maintains that the accused was present for this exchange. They did not properly put their case on that matter to Colonel Dudley or to Tony Birtley or to Ejub Guster. And secondly I want to emphasise the importance of the presence, the alleged presence according to Colonel Tucker, of Morillon and Mihajlov at that exchange, because it's not simply that we say that Colonel Tucker made a mistake too about those people, who you recall would have had to travel in the same APC as Colonel Dudley to the site of the exchange. But the fact that Tucker according to his evidence, his reason for thinking that the accused was there was partly based at least on what Mihajlov said, and you can see in the following slide what he said: Colonel Tucker, answer: "I believed correctly or incorrectly," you note allowed the possibility of error there, "that I was seeing Oric but more significantly to me, it was Mihajlov who had the conversation was him and it was, and Mihajlov had said, 'Oric said this,' 'Oric said that,'" et cetera. "So it never occurred to me that this might be anyone else and, to be honest, because I'm here, I did not personally carry out the conversations with Colonel Oric because obviously I didn't speak Serbo-Croat. But Mihajlov did, and I would find it surprising if Mihajlov in speaking with somebody would realise that he was speaking with somebody else." So a lot of what Tucker says about that exchange depends on Mihajlov being there. And Mihajlov, as we know, was the bodyguard or aide de camp of General Morillon. They went everyone together. If Morillon isn't there at the exchange, if Mihajlov isn't there, then it's obvious Colonel Tucker's account is mistaken and neither Mihajlov nor Morillon were there, according to Dudley, Birtley, and Guster. So on the accused's presence in the exchange of 007, Tucker could not be more mistaken and Your Honours will certainly fall into error if you find that the accused was there. Thirdly, Ms. Richardson said I think it was Tuesday, that it would have been quite useful if we had shown the video of D1010 of the exchange to Colonel Tucker when he was here. Well, as we made very clear in our final brief, it was explicit, we found that video during the Defence phase. And I only wish we had it in order to show it to Colonel Tucker, because it may have changed his evidence about the accused's presence entirely. And as I say, I certainly hope that the Prosecution does not have that video anywhere in their archives. On the law of murder the Prosecution contradicts itself when dealing with prove case and murder. It states without citing any authority, "provocation is not a defence recognised in international law." That's paragraph 6 of the response. But then they say "a mere verbal insult is legally insufficient to provoke murder." First that formula is question begging because if provocation applies, it's not murder but manslaughter, but second, saying that a verbal insult is legally insufficient implies that the matter is indeed regulated by law which the Prosecution had just denied. Our submissions remain on provocation, and particularly on the injustice that a charge of murder against this accused should turn on facts completely outside his knowledge, namely on whether or not Kemo was sufficiently provoked to lose his self control by Kukic. If there was even a possibility that Kemo killed Kukic unintentionally in a furious moment when he saw red after Kukic said "Fuck your Ustasha mother," then that should take it out of the realm of murder. I turn now to cruel treatment. The Prosecution states that the mental element of cruel treatment includes both direct and indirect intent but that's not what is stated in the case law. A standard definition of cruel treatment is given in the Celebici trial judgement at paragraph 517, and it's very clear. "An intentional act or omission which causes serious mental or physical suffering or injury or constitutes a serious attack on human dignity." There is no mention of indirect intent. Also on cruel treatment the Prosecution says that we accept that "detainees were subjected to inhumane conditions of detention." Now, this is a typical gross distortion of what we said in our brief. What we said and it's on the next slide, I believe, is at paragraph 227. I won't read out the whole paragraph but you'll see from that that we needed admitted cruel treatment in our closing brief nor do we seek to excuse the fact that were often cold and did not have ample food. It's a question of what could be done for those people. Thousands of people were starving to death in Srebrenica in 1992 to 1993 because the Serbs were not letting food in. They were freezing to death because it was a bitterly cold winter, the Serbs had cut off the electricity and there was no [indiscernible] fuel to be had. No one in Srebrenica had proper sanitation or a clean water supply. Now, these things could not be conjured up out of thin air for the Serb detainees and that's our point and it's an obvious one: The law does not require people do the impossible. I turn to wanton destruction. On the law which applies to wanton destruction the Prosecution in its closing brief invokes the notion of indiscriminate attacks and states that we did not address it. Well, we did not address it because the accused is not charged with launching indiscriminate attacks. He's charged with wanton destruction. And the Prosecution should reread their own indictment and remind themselves of what crimes the accused is charged with. Now my colleague set out the correct approach to be taken with respect to wanton destruction under additional protocol 1 in terms of first determining, the first test is to determine whether the attack was on a military objective, and, second, to see whether any damage caused was incidental to that legitimate attack. She also addressed the issue of who bears the burden of proving that any damage done was not incidental to an attack on a military objective and that that damage was done by the accused's subordinates. The burden is on the Prosecution to prove these matters beyond a reasonable doubt. In its brief in response the Prosecution's ultimate fall back is, well, no attack should have been launched on these villages. That rather than risking damage to Serb property, the Muslims in Srebrenica should have stayed in the basements and cellars where they were sheltering from Serb shelling and simply died, starved to death. There is no law against dying, only fighting back. I'm sure the people of Srebrenica are glad that they were defended by people of Oric's ilk and not people with that attitude because that's simply a chance for defeatists. It's a counsel for lambs to be led to slaughter rather than to resist. Not once has the Prosecution proposed a realistic standard or model for analysing the unique problems posed by the warfare, the terrain, and the presence of thousands of starving civilians in Srebrenica. And why would they? For the Prosecution, in Srebrenica it was only ever a "so-called siege." That's the express they use in their response between paragraphs 13 and 14 and I invite the public to see that. According to the Prosecution it was not a real siege. What would a real siege be according to the Prosecution? I can't imagine what it would take, how much worse the situation would have to be, before the Prosecution would admit that the poor people of Srebrenica were under siege. I wonder whether for them, whether Sarajevo was under siege, and I wonder if I see a phrase like the "so-called siege of Srebrenica," almost mocking, whether the Prosecution has lost its moral compass altogether. I turn now to aiding and abetting and the elements of that form of liability. Aiding and abetting, Your Honours is only mentioned in the indictment and in the Prosecution's pre-trial brief in relation to count 5 of the indictment. It was not cited and it cannot be called in aid for any of the other counts in the indictment. Our whole strategy at trial is based on what the Prosecution set out in its indictment and in its pre-trial brief. We have never had to consider aiding and abetting in relation to the detention charges. And I'll return to that subject shortly. In terms of the elements for aiding and abetting the Prosecution says that there is no authority for the proposition that for aiding and abetting the accused's contribution must be direct. There is ample authority, and I refer to the Tadic trial decision 7th of May 1997, paragraphs 689 to 692 for the direct and substantial formula is used. And it's also used in the Celebici trial judgement. At paragraph 326. It's worth recalling how serious the crimes are under the ICTY statute. It does a disservice to this body of law to seek continually to water down the elements that need to be proved so that everyone is caught in the web of criminal liability. The law is held in higher esteem if the appropriate high thresholds are applied and not circumvented. And it's in that spirit that I turn to the law of command responsibility and I say that nothing will do more to undermine the esteem in which international humanitarian law is held than by overextending the concept of command responsibility. We do well to remember the origins of command responsibility, an extremely well organised armies, the Japanese and German armies during second world war with uniformed soldiers organised into ranks with barracks, units, and presided over by military commanders with decades of experience and with all the rules, regulations, courts, necessary to maintain discipline. And then in those cases, massive crimes, tens of thousands of people killed, Yamashita, for example, thousands of people killed, civilians in Manila under the watch of those commanders. That's what command responsibility evolved to deal with. It did not evolve as a matter of strict liability by which a commander is responsible for every single act by anybody, man, woman or child, whether he knows about it or not. If that is what the Prosecution would have the law be and I've tried to trace the potential liability of a commander under their theory of command responsibility as set out in the final brief. And it reminds me of that song, "I danced with a man who danced with the girl who danced with the Prince of Wales." It's an endless daisy chain of liability whereby a commander is responsible for what someone else did in respect to helping someone else who might have incited someone else to plan, to aid. It goes on and on. And according to the Prosecution if a commander had some information, not even information of a crime being committed by his subordinates, but some vague, general information of the subordinate being about to plan, to aid and abet another, to instigate, the attempted commission by another of the crime of incitement, it goes on and on. That's not the law. Nor has it ever been. Let's recall what the Celebici Trial Chamber said on this subject. "Great care must be taken, great care must be taken, lest an injustice be committed in holding individuals responsible for the acts of others in situations where the link of control is absent or too remote." Absent or too remote. And now if the law of command responsibility with were as proposed by the Prosecution, would anyone respect it? Would people take seriously a law which dispenses with the most elementary requirements of legality, of clarity, and of distinctly defined mens rea and acts reus? They would not. Now the Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal is increasingly cautious about applying theories of criminal responsibility which cannot clearly be shown to exist under customary international law, and I refer to the Appeals Chamber's decision on interlocutory appeal challenging jurisdiction in relation to command responsibility in Hadzihasanovic-Kubura dated 16 July 2003, and I believe we have a slide. Yes. "The Appeals Chamber holds view that this Tribunal can pose criminal liability only if the crime charged was clearly established under customary law at the time the events in issue occurred. In case of doubt, criminal responsibility cannot be found to exist. Thereby preserving full respect for the principle of legality." And that's exactly how it should be. And in that same decision, indeed in the same paragraph in applying this approach the Appeals Chamber held that "an accused cannot be charged under Article 7(3) of the Statute for crimes committed by a subordinate before the said accused assumed command over that subordinate. And that's an important binding holding by the Appeals Chamber to which I shall return. Your Honours the Tribunal has one sure instrument for command responsibility and that's Article 7(3) of the Statute. And that deals with the responsibility of a superior for crimes committed or about to be committed by his subordinates. Nothing more. It does not cover liability of a superior for his subordinates' aiding and abetting crimes. Only committing crimes. Now the Trial Chamber so held in the Blagojevic judgement of 17 January 2005 and it's paragraph 794. Now the Prosecution is appealing the Trial Chamber's judgement but the Trial Chamber correctly stated the law and that's the law of the Tribunal, and Your Honours can be safely guided by it. The Prosecution has not proved that subordinates of the accused committed murder or cruel treatment and has not proved under Article 7(3) that subordinates of the accused perpetrated crimes in the SUP or in the building and the accused is therefore entitled to an acquittal on the counts relating to detention. Now I'll return to that subject in more detail after addressing some other features of the Prosecution's approach to command responsibility. Concerning the mens rea requirement the Prosecution contends that there is no requirement that the superior's "negligence was so serious as to amount to malicious intent." Again, there is abundant authority for this and the Prosecution cannot be so ignorant of the law and if they know of it it's a breach of their duty to the Court to suggest, even to suggest that there is no authority. The fundamental authority is from the official commentaries to additional protocol 1 by Claude Pilleau [phoen] et al.
