And if we recall that Article 7(3) of the Statute is actually based on Article 86 of additional protocol 1, and that's the conventional source for Article 7(3), we see how important the commentary on that Article is. And the commentary says this: This does not mean that every case of negligence is criminal. For this to be so, the negligence must be so serious that it is tantamount to malicious intent. So there they are, the exact words we used, malicious intent. "The negligence must be so serious that it is tantamount to malicious intent apart from any link between the conduct in question and the damage that took place. "This element in criminal law is far from being clarified but it is essential, essential, since this is precisely on the question of intent that the system of penal sanctions in the conventions is based." Now those words are terribly important in my submission, the system of penal sanctions in the Geneva Conventions is based on the question of intent and that in turn is essential. Now, Your Honours, the Tribunal has not always adhered to those words, and I hesitate to say that it may prove to be one of the major legal mistakes in this Tribunal to convict people of intent-like crimes, like murder and rape, when they had no intent. And you will have noticed that national jurisdictions implementing Article 28 of the Rome Statute, the equivalent of Article 7(3) are very wary of how they are adopted into their domestic legislation. Many nations recognising the injustice of penalising what Professor Chavez [phoen] calls, "the commission of a crime of intent by negligence," have enacted a separate crime of dereliction of duty where they prosecute command responsibility only when there is an intentional element. And as Your Honour Judge Eser will be aware, under section 4 of the German code of crimes against international law [German spoken], "the criminal responsibility of a superior can only be incurred nor an intentional, [German spoken] omission to prevent a subordinate from committing a crime. And these positions in national law fit far better with what was said about the required mens rea in the first cases on command responsibility, and that this is what was said in USA versus Wilhelm von Leeb, the high command case, and that's 27 October 1948. I won't read the whole extract. But you see there the important part, "there must be a personal dereliction by the commander "that can only occur -- that can occur only when the act is directly traceable to him or where his failure proper toy to supervise his subordinates constitutes criminal negligence on his part. In the latter case it must be a personal neglect amounting to a wanton immoral disregard of the action of his subordinates amounting to acquiescence. Any other interpretation of international law would go far beyond the basic principles of criminal law known to civilised nations." Now these words are highly important to bear in mind and a caution against adopting the watered-down approach favoured by the Prosecution which does basically equate to strict liability, ultimately. And why do we say it equates to strict liability? Let me take an example. According to the Prosecution a superior has inquiry notice of a crime if he could just potentially have access to information about a crime being committed. And according to the Prosecution, having access includes when the subordinate knows of the crime and the accused doesn't consult him. But if that were true, then every time a subordinate committed a crime the accused would per se have inquiry notice of the crime, strict liability. You'll find a pattern here. Whenever the Prosecution sets out its interpretation of command responsibility, it tries to push it towards strict liability and away from any form of intent. And now, they are even trying to push command responsibility away from responsibility for subordinates towards responsibility for third parties. Now that is utterly contrary to basic principles of criminal law and the intentions of the drafters of additional protocol 1 and the framers of the first dock drinks of command responsibility after World War II, and moreover the malicious intent standard has been affirmed by the Rwanda Tribunal in its very first judgement. And I refer Your Honour to paragraphs 488 to 489 of the Akayesu trial judgement of the 2nd of September 1998. There is another very important principle in relation to the mens rea requirement for command responsibility which the Appeals Chamber set out in their Krnojelac appeal judgment, 17 September 2003, and, Your Honour Judge Agius, will, of course be familiar with that judgement because you sat on the panel, as I believe. The Prosecution argued in that case that in order to have inquiry notice, the information received by the superior need not point to any specific crime; the superior need only receive information of a general nature, putting him on notice of the risk of crimes being committed. And the Appeals Chamber, after reviewing the case law, had this to say. It's at paragraph 155. Now since it's on the slide I won't read it and I simply refer the Trial Chamber to that extract but the gist of it is information about beatings does not equate to information about torture, if I may summarise it that way. And thus the Trial Chamber said "it is not enough that an accused has sufficient information about beatings inflicted by his subordinates, he must also have information, albeit general, which alerts him to the risk of beatings being inflicted for one of the purposes provided for in the prohibition against torture inquiry." Now the same reasoning applies to this case and the question about cruel treatment, the first offence, and information about murder, second offence. Information about the first does not equate to information about the latter. Now I turn now to the command responsibility issues arising specifically -- my apologies, Your Honour
