utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. My apologies, Your Honours, and my apologies to the interpreters. The next slide we have a diagram which is to illustrate the Prosecution's theory of the case as it now emerges, not even in the Prosecution final brief but for the very first time in their response to our closing brief. In its response the Prosecution argues for the very first time that the accused may be held responsible for crimes committed by what we call opportunistic visitors to the prison and I'll use prison for shorthand for the SUP or the building by virtue of Article 7(1), and in that regard we make three points: That such an approach is ultra vires the Statute, that it was not pleaded, and it certainly hasn't been proved. I refer Your Honours again to the indictment and the pre-trial brief. You will see that aiding and abetting is nowhere argued, Article 7(1) is no where cited in relation to the detention charges, only in relation to the wanton destruction of Fakovici, Bjelovac, and Kravica, and Jezestica on the 7th of January. Now it's a fundamental principle of a fair criminal trial that the Accused knows the charges that he has to answer, in fact, and in law, before the trial commences. And I cannot emphasise that point strongly enough. The Tribunal's case law amply sets out the requirement for all material elements to be pleaded in the indictment, and this has recently been confirmed in the Hadzihasanovic-Kubura trial judgement at paragraph 269. And I would also refer Your Honours to that judgement in its entirety for its many important dicta on command responsibility. So since nowhere in the indictment or the pre-trial brief did the Prosecution argue that the Defence or Your Honours would have to consider aiding and abetting and the elements of aiding and abetting in relation to the detention charges, we were not on notice that the Prosecution would be making that argument. It was not pleaded. The Prosecution has only thought of using Article 7(1) in relation to the detention charges recently, and it is not permitted to raise that for the first time after all the evidence that is been heard. Nonetheless since this argument has been raised I feel obliged to respond to it. Now, we, of course, do not accept that the accused was the superior of the guards at the SUP or at the building. These locations were under the control of the civilian police within which the military police was located, and under control of the War Presidency, and I refer Your Honours to paragraphs 532 to 549 of our closing brief. We also reject that the accused had de jure or de facto authority over the military police in Srebrenica. And that's dealt with at paragraphs 584 to 682 of our closing brief. And the points made in those paragraphs are barely addressed by the Prosecution, and again I invite Your Honours to note our arguments there and the evidence we cite and to infer that since the Prosecution has no convincing rebuttal to the evidence cited and the points made, that it's because they have no explanation. So the issue set out in the schema does not in any event arise on the facts but we address it for the sake of argument. Now if the accused were the superior of guards at the two prison locations, or the guards themselves did not commit murder or cruel treatment but rather opportunistic visitors then you'll note the following, first the perpetrators are unknown and you will note in this regard that in the Blagojevic trial judgement at paragraph 794 the Trial Chamber precluded command responsibility for unknown perpetrators. Second, the perpetrators do not even belong to an identifiable group which could even arguably be under the command of the accused. They are just unidentified individual perpetrators. And Your Honours yourselves emphasised the need and this was in your 98 bis decision for unidentified perpetrators to at least be members of some identifiable group subordinated to the accused. In this scheme, you'll see that there is no link between the accused and the actual perpetrators of the crimes. The perpetrators are not even argued to be the accused's subordinates or under his effective control. The subordinates are not the perpetrators of the crimes. And so to attribute criminal responsibility to the accused would, as we said in our closing brief, be a, what we termed a double-normative attribution use, "obejektive Zurechnung," I believe may be the term in German. Horizontally via Article 7(1) to reach the subordinates, and then vertically via Article 7(3) to finally reach the accused on the Prosecution's theory. Now this double-normative attribution is not contemplated by the Statute and it would be considered ultra vires in any civilised system of law. Now I wish to emphasise 3 points in this regard. This is -- Article 7(3) clearly covers liability only for subordinates committing crimes, not for all the inchoate forms of liability. Now this submission is borne out by three considerations, at least. First, that's the holding in the Blagojevic judgement, and that judgement was explicit. The accused's subordinates had "rendered practical assistance that furthered the crimes of murder and extermination." But the subordinates had not committed the crimes themselves and that meant that one could not say whom the accused had a duty to punish. In Blagojevic was there ever been acquitted in relation to those counts. Now, if the Prosecution does rely on crimes perpetrated by visitors to the prisons, whom do they say the accused was under a duty to punish? Under Article 7(3) the only duty could be to punish the guards. But punish for what? For letting people into the prison to mistreat prisoners? Yet there is no evidence that the Accused ever received any information that that was happening. And there is no evidence, not one line of transcript or one exhibit, which the Prosecution can point to, to show that the accused knew that guards at the two prison locations were letting people into those locations to mistreat prisoners and that in itself should be an end to the story. If you'll forgive me, Your Honours, my screen is frozen. Second, Article 7(3) refers in its own terms to committing, not participating in or perpetrating crimes. Now, third, this submission is borne out by two fundamental principles of statutory interpretation which is set out in the Delalic et al trial judgement paragraph 158 to 171. First of all, the literal interpretation, i.e. interpreting a provision according to its plain meaning, unless that leads to uncertainty or repugnance. Well, the words of Article 7(3) are plain and crystal clear. They cover crimes committed by subordinates, not committed by others and aided and abetted by subordinates. And there is nothing absurd about that result. In its response to our closing brief, Prosecution states at paragraph 28 "the Defence argument assumes that the term committing in Article 7(3) must have the identical meaning to committing under Article 7(1)." Well, that's actually a pretty reasonable assumption, isn't it, that one word has the same meaning when it's used in the same article of the Statute. I don't see anything absurd about that at all. It's for the -- the burden is on the Prosecution to show that that interpretation is absurd. And the burden is also on the Prosecution to show that state practice and opinio juris support its argument that a superior may be held responsible for crimes which were not even committed by his subordinates, and I defy them to find a single precedent. The Prosecution goes on to say, "Nothing in Article 7(3) suggest that liability under that article applies only where a subordinate engaged in criminal conduct only through the committing mode of liability." Well again, nothing suggests it, the plain words of Article 7(3) state it. They prove it beyond doubt. The drafters of Article 7(3) could have used other words, participating or perpetrating, but they didn't. They used the word "committing," and that word committing has been clearly defined by Tribunal jurisprudence to refer to, if we have the slide, "Physically perpetrating a crime or engendering a culpable admission in [indiscernible] criminal law. And that's in the Krstic judgement at paragraph 601, and that definition has been uphold in many other cases. The use the word "or" in Article 7(1), "committing or otherwise aided and abetted," also shows that committing is contrasted from other forms of liability listed there, and particularly contrasted from aiding and abetting. Committing is utterly distinct from aiding and abetting as wealth as from planning, instigating, ordering, and joint criminal enterprise. As Article 7(1) and that paragraph from Krstic makes clear, that since it goes on to define all the other forms of liability. So does Article 2 of Statute make it clear that committing or ordering to be committed. Committing is not used in the Statute, as the Prosecution suggests, as a broad term to cover all forms of criminal liability. The other fundamental principle, of statutory interpretation is in dubio pro reo, namely if there is any doubt, it's to be resolved in favour of the Accused. Now the Prosecution raises a host of objections to this careful and correct position held in Blagojevic that Article 7(3) is limited to committing. None of them are convincing. And I'll deal with those arguments one by one, but first an overview of the Statute will help set things in order. The crimes in the ICTY Statute are set out in Articles 2 to 5. Article 7 is not a crime-creating or jurisdiction-conferring article. It sets out forms of liability in the crimes set out in Articles 2 to 5. And there are two separate pillars, Article 7(1) and Article 7(3). You can be responsible for those crimes through 7(1) or through command responsibility under 7(3). Article 7(3) does not refer to Article 7(1) and Article 7(1) does not refer to Article 7(3). They are self standing independent pillars of criminal liability. This was recently confirmed in the judgement of Hadzihasanovic-Kubura. It says there, [French spoken] Article 7(3) is a sui generis, a unique responsibility, and distinct from that provided for by Article 7(1) of the Statute. Yet the Prosecution argues that whenever committing appears in the Statute it's shorthand for all the other forms of liability in Article 7(1). And there is nothing to support such an argument. It were so then Article 2 would not refer to committing or ordering to be committed. Article 4 on genocide would be nonsensical because it states that conspiracy to commit genocide and direct and public incitement to commit genocide are also punishable offences as well as the other acts when committed with genocidal intent. But according to the Prosecution, it would be unnecessary to state all that and because committing can simply be read to include all those forms any way. Prosecution relies on Articles 1, 9 and 29 of the Statute to justify their argument. But the appeal to these articles is also unsustainable. As a matter of territorial jurisdiction it's a requirement of the Statute be committed on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and that means physically committed on the territory. If a crime were committed elsewhere, let's say in the United Kingdom, but aided and abetted in the former Yugoslavia that would not fall within the competence of this Tribunal. So committing -- "committed" there means physically committed. And that's why Article 1 and Article 9 refer to crimes committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. As for Article 29 that doesn't concern jurisdiction or criminal responsibility and in fact it doesn't even use the word committed but committing in the English version. The Prosecution would have to rely on the French version to make its point. Article 29 moreover is not -- it's a poorly drafted provision, if I may put it 245 way because it should also refer to crimes committed on the territory of the former Yugoslavia since states are not obliged to assist its Tribunal in its investigation of any crimes committed anywhere. So the whole body of the Prosecution's controversial theory on Article 7(3) that commit something shorthand for all the other forms of liability cannot be supported by the reference to one poorly chosen word in the French version of a non-substantive Article of the Statute dealing with state cooperation. Since the Prosecution's theory fails as a matter of statutory interpretation the Prosecution argues that a literal interpretation of Article 7(3) would lead to illogical results because a commander is obliged to prevent any criminal conducts by his subordinates. But that is completely question begging. It begs the very question of whether Article 7(3) does indeed cover all the other forms of criminal conduct. That's a boot strapping argument. If a commander did know that his subordinates were planning to aid and abet others to commit crimes and he did nothing he may well be liable under conventional theories of criminal liability. His omission to act may be a type of accomplice liability or of instigation or conspiracy, depending on the circumstances. The facts might also be an appropriate case for joint criminal enterprise. But in any event, if there is a gap in the law, the requirements of legality and the requirement that crimes prosecuted by the ICTY be clearly defined in customary law - and I would argue in conventional law, too - means the Prosecution cannot simply justify any extension of the law as a filling-in exercise or as a tidying-up exercise. It has to provide solid precedent to justify its radical interpretation of Article 7(3) which would make a person responsible for crimes committed by throws over whom he was no effective control. Second, even leaving all of that aside, even if the law did allow such an interpretation, it was not pleaded in this case. I won't dwell on that, Your Honours. I think I've made that point sufficiently clear. Third, and finally and as demonstrated in our closing brief there is a complete absence of evidence as to how in fact opportunistic visitors entered the two detention locations. Did they break in, as suggested by some evidence? Was there a lock at either of the locations which someone negligently failed to lock? Or was there no lock at all? When did people get into the prison? And who specifically let them in? Did the people who let them in do it wilfully or negligently? Were they asleep or drunk when people got in? Or were they forced or threatened and acted under duress and therefore without the requisite intention? Why did visitors have to beat the prisoners through the bars? Was it because the guards tried to stop abuse by keeping the cells locked? Were there other incidents like those mentioned by Ratko Nikolic where the guards tried to prevent mistreatment of detainees? Your Honours will recall that Mr. Radic testified, "Nobody touched us by day. We were left alone." Well, were the guards even still on duty at night? There is a complete evidential void on the subject. In sum, we simply do not know how, why, under what circumstances, visitors gained access to the detention premises because no evidence has been brought on the matter. Now the Prosecution could have called a guard or a perpetrator or someone who would have explained how it came to be and you'll see that in other cases you'll have evidence from guards and from visitors saying I was let in or there was a general knowledge that this was happening and the camp commander knew that people were breaking in. You'll -- these are not necessary evidential voids, they are filled in, in most cases but not in this case. And so, Your Honours, you can not simply go for the worst assumption from a whole universe of assumptions, namely that the guards must have acted as co-perpetrators with the visitors and intentionally let them in to beat and kill prisoners. Since you can't find that, the guards cannot be liable for murder and cruel treatment, and so neither can the accused through Article 7(3). Finally, Your Honours, and I make this only as a fallback submission if Your Honours were not to accept any of the arguments that I just made, I submit that you still could find the accused guilty as there has been no proof, not a single tittle of evidence that the accused knew the guards were letting opportunistic visitors into the prison to mistreat detainees. And the Hadzihasanovic-Kubura judgement deals with the fact that knowledge does have to be of a certain level of specificity. And certainly if this is the mechanism by which crimes were committed, guards letting people in, then it must be proved that the accused knew that was happening. Or at least was even on inquiry notice that that was happening. Now the only identified perpetrator of any of the crimes is Kemo, according to the evidence of Radic. And I won't rehearse all the evidence on Kemo. It's set out in our closing brief. But I will make one point. That Kemo was not under the accused's effective control is, again, the evidence of Prosecution witness Dr. Mujkanovic, who was categorical on the subject, and that the Prosecution seems to think that they can ignore that evidence too. And again, that's evidence we relied on, and perhaps we would have called witnesses to deal with Kemo if we ever dreamt that the Prosecution would be allowed to depart from what its own witness said. Regarding documents relied on by the Prosecution relating to the Pale Territorial Defence, none of them shows that Kemo was the accused's subordinate, much less that he was his subordinate on the 25th of September, 1992, the day that Kukic was killed according to Radic, and, Your Honours, that's why I referred earlier to a section of -- I believe it was the Kunarac judgement, that, of course, the subordinate has to be a subordinate at the date that the crimes were committed by him. And as the Appeals Chamber held in the Kunarac judgement, paragraph 399, "To be held liable for the acts of men who operated under him on an ad hoc or temporary basis, it must be shown that at the time when the acts charged in the indictment were committed these persons were under the effective control of the accused." And the Chamber referred to the Appeals Chamber's judgement in Celebici, paragraphs 197 to 198 and 256. Now, Your Honours will recall the abundant evidence of witnesses, including Hakija Meholjic who was emphatic on this point, that people changed groups all the time. They could drift back and forth between groups of fighters as they liked. So in these circumstances, it's crucial to know when someone was in a group in order to find that he was a subordinate. So even if the Kemo who killed Kukic is Kemo Mehmetovic rather than Kemo Ahmetovic as claimed by Radic, none of the Prosecution's exhibits show that he was the accused's subordinate on the 25th of September, 1992. Now on the subject of Kemo, you will recall that it was he, not the accused, who, according to Radic, came into the cell when Kukic's body was there. Now in our response to the final brief we pointed out the Prosecution had misstated the evidence on that point, and in fact, we pointed out 13 major misstatements of the evidence, mischaracterisations on crucial matters, not a mere slip of the pen, and we said this at paragraph 27 of our response: "The Prosecution has misstated the evidence on critical matters, the Defence calls upon the Prosecution immediately to concede that the examples below are errors or the Defence will be forced to conclude that the Prosecution is deliberately seeking to mislead the Chamber on the evidence and to secure convictions on an erroneous basis." Now that was on the 24th of March, 2006, nearly two weeks ago. You've heard two days of Prosecution closing arguments. They made partial admissions on two points that they had mischaracterised the evidence, one regarding the accused's presence in the cell and one regarding Ahmo Tihic. I'm going to come to the way in which they -- they tried to cover that mistake in a moment, but they have not admitted that they misstated the evidence on the following points: False statements about the accused allegedly taking Sarac from the SUP; false statements about visitors to the prison; false statements about Mirzet Halilovic being subordinated to the accused; false statements about the accused's presence during beatings of Ivanovic in the building; their confusion about what happened in Cerska with what happened in Srebrenica; misstatements about identification of the accused by Sarac, as if he were a witness; misstatements about Nikolic being escorted to the SUP by the accused; misrepresentations about the black Mercedes; misrepresentations about Hakija Meholjic; misrepresentations in regard to P84; misrepresentations about the Gotic [phoen] incident; and misrepresentations about the accused's interview and relying on witnesses' comments on mistranslated parts of the interview. The Prosecution hasn't come clean on any of those matters and said, "Yes, we regret, we apologise. Those were mistakes." And so, Your Honours, the invitation remains to your Trial Chamber to infer that the Prosecution indeed wishes you to rely on the misstated position in its brief rather than the true position. And let's see how they corrected the mistake, if it is a mistake, about Naser Oric being in the cell with Mr. Kukic. This is what they said at paragraph 362 of the Prosecution final brief: "Mr. Kukic's dead body was returned to the cell and remained there until 10:00 a.m. the next morning when Oric arrived and asked what had happened." Now, Ms. Sellers said that that was simply -- simply a full stop which wasn't inserted and that, actually, that should appear between the word "morning" and "when." So it would be: "Mr. Kukic's dead body was returned to the cell and remained there until 10 a.m. the next morning," full stop. "When Oric arrived and asked what happened." Well, I'm sorry, that's not a sentence, and that's obviously not the explanation. And I invite you to find that Ms. Sellers has not provided you with a candid explanation about that misstatement of the evidence. It would have been better if she simply said that they confused Kemo and Oric rather than offering an explanation which is clearly untrue. And so for that misstatement and the others, I invite you to infer, and the Prosecution's lack of condor in admitting that these are errors, even after we pointed them out and invited them to, that they wish to mislead you on the evidence. As far as other alleged visitors to the SUP and the building are concerned, I would just add a couple of words. Zulfo Tursunovic, you'll recall that the Prosecution's own evidence is that he was an independent character who would do his own thing. As Meholjic said, who knew him and the accused well and had many dealings with them both, "Zulfo was not accountable to anyone." And that's 8th of April, 2005, T6948. Not a single witness has testified that Tursunovic received orders from the accused or that he reported to him. There is not one document in which Tursunovic reports to the accused, nor has any evidence been given that he reported to the accused orally. There is simply no evidence that Zulfo Tursunovic was under the effective control of the accused at any time. Now when there is no evidence, the Prosecution just invites you to assume that key facts have been proved. So it is with Hamed Salihovic. At paragraph 92 of the Prosecution's response we read this: "Salihovic necessarily reported the information derived from the prisoners to Oric." Well, what does that mean, "necessarily reported"? Why has the word "necessarily" been interinserted? Because there is no evidence that he did so report. Not a single document has been tendered in evidence in which Salihovic reported information derived from prisoners to the accused. No witness testified that Salihovic reported to the accused. You would think that that would bother the Prosecution, but not a bit of it. They'll just tell you to assume that it happened. In fact, the Prosecutor's own evidence shows that Salihovic ordered the military police around in his capacity, it was assumed capacity, as president of the subregion, president of the subregion War Presidency. And that's Prosecution Exhibit P12 -- P212. So, in fact, the evidence tends to show that Salihovic regarded the accused as his subordinate, as he was before the war, rather than as his superior. Now, Your Honours, I turn now to the issue of -- issues of identification. The Prosecution knows how poor the alleged identification evidence is in this case. So its approach is to tell Your Honour that you needn't be too worried about the dangers of misidentification. This despite all the remarks made by the Appeals Chamber in Kupreskic about the need for extreme caution as well as in the recent Limaj judgement. The Prosecution would lead you straight into the very errors about which these Chambers have cautioned. Now, Ms. Richardson, on Tuesday, said that we had erroneously relied on the dicta in Kupreskic and on the Turnbull guidelines. This is an astonishing remark. Those cases set up guidelines, essential guidelines as to how to approach identification evidence. There is no question of relying on them erroneously. Identification is in issue in this case so the guidelines apply. And the questions posed in Turnbull are terribly important. They are vital for the Trial Chamber to consider. "How long did the witness have the accused under observation, at what distance, in what light? Was the observation impeded in any way? Had the witness ever seen the accused before? How long elapsed between the original observation and the subsequent identification to the police? Was there any material discrepancy between the description of the accused given to the police when first seen by them and his actual appearance? Every single one of those questions is vital for Your Honours to consider in relation to the evidence of the detention witnesses. And in fact, the identification evidence in this case, is in every respect of the very worst kind when one considers the Turnbull guidelines. That's why the Prosecution doesn't want you to consider them. So Ms. Richardson sought to distinguish guideline cases on the facts of those cases, which shows that she simply doesn't understand what guideline cases are about. They are not about the facts of those cases. They are cited for the guidelines. And listening to Ms. Richardson trying to distinguish Turnbull and Kupreskic on their facts, you would think there were at least three additional witnesses who testified here. I had to check the Prosecution exhibits -- sorry, the Prosecution witness list to make sure. I've established that Veselin Ceric was not a witness in this case. He never gave evidence. He never testified. Yet that's what she would have you believe, if you look in LiveNote Tuesday page 53, line 22, Mr. Sarac testified, page 52 line 8, she referred to witness Mr. Sarac. "If Sarac had testified under oath, I would have had a lot to put to him in cross-examination, for example whether he really is from Srebrenica or from Podravanje, as Radic has testified." "How he in fact claims to know the Accused from before the war when the Accused was most of the time in Potocari and Belgrade, where they met and how often. I would also ask him about the two untrue statement that is Radic attributed to him on the video, P98. I would ask him about what is edited out of that video as I asked Mr. Radic." "And I would ask him when he had this conversation with Oric," about being hit by him when apparently the last time they saw each other was when that very hitting took place. Sarac did not testify. He was not a witness, nor was Dustana [phoen] a witness, as Ms. Richardson suggested. No witness recognised the accused as someone they knew before the war. The third witness who was not a witness was the accused. He never testified and I simply refer you to what my colleague said and what we said in our motion in our closing brief, about the probative value which can be given to that deeply flawed piece of evidence which not even an investigator authenticated or testified about in any way. No one came forward to say that that was properly done, properly conducted. We were not able to cross-examine an investigator about any of those matters. So the Prosecution states that Defence "overemphasised the dangers involved in relying on identification evidence". I find that profoundly depressing as a remark because the Prosecution itself should be concerned about convicting an innocent man based on shaky identification evidence. Royal commissions were set up and guidelines issued and judicial pronouncements made around the world exactly to counter that complacent attitude which has led to so many miscarriages of justice, to so many innocent people being wrongly convicted. Now the issue of identification is dealt with at length in our closing brief so I'll just reiterate the basic facts. First, we are talking about few and fleeting alleged sightings of the accused 12 years ago under the worst possible conditions for observation: In dark cells, in winter, when there was no electricity, when the detainees were confused and disorientated. Prosecution witnesses said how during daylight hours there was not enough light in the cells to recognise an individual's details. The Prosecution has not conducted a single identification parade or identification procedure to check whether the alleged identification evidence is at all satisfactory or reliable. Now, that's a glaring omission in a case which depends on identification evidence. And the detention charges do depend on identification evidence to establish inquiry notice. As I say, none of the witnesses who testified about seeing the accused knew him from before the war, so none of them recognised him as someone they knew. Conversely, the accused receives extensive public exposure on television and in newspapers in the former Yugoslavia. Many witnesses said how they saw the accused on television and in photos since the war. There is all the talk that can be expected in small Serb communities about the accused and this trial. Your Honours will be well aware of the dangers of suggestion created by these factors. And in that regard, it's highly pertinent to point out that out of 12 detention witnesses, 11 of them either did not testify at trial that they saw or heard about Naser Oric when in detention or did not do so in their earlier statements about events. Eleven out of 12 witnesses. Now, is this simply a question of a few links in the Prosecution's chain armour failing, or is it the whole fabric falling apart before Your Honours' eyes? None of the witnesses were able to point to any distinctive characteristics in alleged identifications of the accused. What they pointed to characteristics, they were wrong. Of the five witnesses who claimed to have seen Naser Oric in either the SUP or the building, three, Radic, Zikic, and Mitrovic, describe him as being clean-shaven or having no beard. Yet the incontrovertible evidence is the accused wore a beard for the entire period. Let's recall what Radic said about the poor lighting in the cells in the SUP and the difficulties of observation. I have a slide which sets that out. "Question: You've told us that a lot of the time you were in the prison that the cell was very dark; is that right? "Answer: Yes, yes. At night, obviously, there was no electricity, and even by day there was a small opening in the wall, some sort of a window. 60 by 50 centimetres by was the size, and that was the only opening for the light to come into the cell. "Question: And this was September, October, so coming on for winter. Is it right that the days were very short, so it was dark both in the mornings -- early mornings and early evening? "Answer: Yes. "Question: So in fact it was very hard to see any real detail of people's faces in the cell? "Answer: It was difficult to see, that's one thing. Secondly, there were no visible injuries on our faces." And Your Honours know the significance of that. "Question: So in fact when you looked out from your cell you were looking into even greater darkness? "Answer: Yes." Now, is that evidence which the Turnbull guidelines don't address, which can be safely ignored? No. It's absolutely critical for Your Honours in deciding whether or not Radic was able to identify the accused. And on top of all that, we have uncontested evidence from several Prosecution witnesses, as well as Defence, that many people in Srebrenica adopted the look of the accused during the relevant period, and that at least one individual played on the resemblance to pretend to be him. And incidentally, I would point out the Prosecution has confused two different Mrkis in its response to our final brief and in its closing speech and I submit that that will be obvious when you see the evidence of Dr. Mujkanovic, that there were at least three Mrkis in Srebrenica. And when you look at the evidence of Mr. Radic referring to Mrki as being "very tall, over two metres, a big burly man" - that's T3519 - and Stojanovic referring to him as, "He wasn't very tall." In our submissions, it's a different Mrki altogether. It's not Hazim Mrki, who Radic identifies with Kemo. Then we have the "actual identifications" of the accused. Radic said that the accused was 160, 70 -- sorry, 160 centimetres tall, with blue eyes and no beard. The accused is 180 centimetres - that's a big difference - has brown eyes and had a beard at the time. Now, how on earth can the Prosecution claim that this is a satisfactory identification on which you can safely rely to convict the accused? He mentions three features, and they are all completely wrong. Zikic also said the accused had no beard and could point to no other physical characteristics. You also recall, in relation to the visits by Naser Oric, allegedly Naser Oric, described by Zikic and Radic that there was a total mismatch in the visits in that Zikic does not describe any of the visits described by Radic and Radic does not describe any of the visits in conversations described by Zikic. Something has gone wrong and at least one of these witnesses is very confused. Your Honours will have to weigh all these major discrepancies and not simply ignore them as the Prosecution has done. Now, turning to the building, Ivanovic was very clear that to this day he's not sure whether he ever laid eyes on the accused in the reception room. He said that several times. He made an assumption based on what some unknown person said to him. Now, when Ms. Richardson summarised his evidence she completely overlooked all the other exchanges which are set out in the next slide. Question: "You didn't mention Naser Oric because you were never sure. To this day you're not sure whether you ever saw him in the prison. It's only an inference you made." Answer: "I said that I could only assume during my captivity in the cell behind the court building that was based on what I heard from the soldiers but I did not know the man personally nor can I say that I recognised him in the reception room." "And today, sitting there where you are, you can't say for sure, can you, whether you ever laid eyes on Naser Oric in the reception room in the prison?" Answer: "I've said this haven't I? I really didn't know him. I confirmed a number of times that I didn't see him." Now if he had recognised Naser Oric subsequently on television, he wouldn't be saying anything like that. He would say I recognised him and I know that that's the man I saw. If we go to the next slide, I put to Mr. Ivanovic: "What we do say is that Naser Oric was not in the reception room in the prison. That's what my questions are concerned with. Do you understand that?" Answer: I fully understand what you mean. As I have said, I don't know him personally. I don't know if he was there. But I think I've explained with sufficient clarity what my assumption was based on. But I did say a number of times that I simply didn't know whether it was him or not." And this is where I clarified that the assumption was nothing to do with images seen on television. It was based on what one identified person said to him. Question: "Yes, you're assumption was based on what the guards said, correct?" Answer: "Yes, precisely." Go to the next slide. He said that, "nor do I want to necessarily link this up," this is referring to an alleged identification "with any images that I may have seen later on." It's crystal clear what the assumption was. Ivanovic was in a room he left he was in the room. He left. Someone said did you see Naser or Delija [phoen] there? We don't know whether that person knew Naser Oric or whether he even knew that he was in the room. Later on television, he heard the name Naser or he saw a picture of someone allegedly being Naser Oric and he assumed that that's the person. If that's a safe basis for convicting the accused, if that's a safe identification, then in my submission something has gone very wrong. Ratko Nikolic who had seen the accused before his arrest, never saw him in detention, never testified seeing him in detention. Now Nikolic was in the reception room with Ivanovic when the accused was allegedly present. The fact that he did not see the accused there when he was seeing exactly what Ivanovic was seeing, it's solid proof that the accused was simply not there. And that is strengthened by the presence of C-07 -- I'm sorry, by the evidence of C-07 who also never said that he heard anything of the accused during his two months of detention. And then you have the women whose evidence does not go to inquiry notice but simply to whether the accused was ever in the prison. Not as to what he would have seen there. Milenija Mitrovic, as we know, referred to hearing of a Naser Kolic [phoen] who came into the cell and was clean shaven and Stana Stamenic provided no physical description of someone who allegedly came into the cell and introduced himself as Naser Oric. Your Honours, that's essentially the sum total of the identification evidence. The dangers are so obvious of relying on this evidence to find that the accused was ever in the SUP or the building that they do not need stating. Now Your Honours the accused was not paying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I saw you looking at your watch. If you wish -- prefer to have a break earlier, you only have to say so. So tell us what your preference is. You still have another 20 minutes before the break, 22 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'm obliged, Your Honour. I noted that I was moving to a new section but since I have 20 minutes that's ample for this section. Your Honours, the accused was not paying regular visits to the SUP or to the building because he had no reason to be there. It was not his bailiwick. On the contrary, he had the most compelling reasons imaginable to be else where, namely on the front lines preventing the Serbs from breaking through and massacring everyone. And throughout this trial whenever we have invoked the spectre of the 95 genocide it was only to make this point, that what happened in July 1995 started happening in April and May 1992 and, as my colleague said yesterday, it could have happened at any time in 1992 or early 1993 if the Serbs took the town. I want Your Honours to imagine yourself in the position of the accused. You'll recall what Prosecution witness Colonel Tucker said of his situation, the Accused's situation when he saw him in March 1993. This is a different quote from the one to which my colleague referred yesterday. I'm not sure if we have a slide on it. He said this: "The people there, particularly the refugees, they believed they were going to die. As I've described previously it was not a question of if, it was only a question of when. Against this background, yes, there was this hero, Naser Oric, but he had very few weapons. He had very few soldiers. The Serbs had many weapons. The Serbs had many soldiers. They didn't believe that he would actually be able to help them and defend them but they believed that he was doing his best." And this was a British Colonel, a Prosecution witness speaking about the Accused with a realism and a compassion for his situation which we have not once heard from the Prosecution during the whole course of this trial. "They believed that he was doing his best." This is a 27 year old finding himself in a hellish world of the Serbs' creation, and I don't know about Your Honours or the Prosecution but at 27 years old my responsibilities were considerably more mundane, focused more on paying off loans than saving hundreds of lives. Colonel Tucker had an eye for military reality, however, as Your Honours will. And so I'd ask Your Honours, when you deliberate, to try to imagine yourself there in Srebrenica among the smells of the thousands of unwashed bodies of refugees, passing by the pile of human limbs outside the war hospital. Seeing as a daily sight, the maimed, the dead, the starving. Losing your young friends every day in fighting the Serbs, and then imagine the imploring looks of the thousands of refugees who rightly or wrongly see you as their salvation. And they are counting on you as the thin wedge between them and the murderous Serb forces and I use that term advisedly because no one can look at Eastern Bosnia in that period and describe the Serb forces as anything less than murderous. To save them from massacre, from rapes, and from going to any place they could go from Srebrenica underground. And I defy anyone to think of a more difficult situation and a more compelling and urgent responsibility than doing everything in your power to stop the Serbs breaking through and killing thousands of innocent civilians. You'll remember that that fear was not one held only by the Bosniaks who had been at the receiving end of the Serbs' violence for nearly a year. UN report also warned on the 20th of March 1993, "if free passage with transport cannot be arranged for the refugees in the Srebrenica pocket within the next 7 to 14 days, indications are that the Serbs will carry out a genocidal cleansing of the entire enclave resulting in the potential death of up to 80.000 human beings." That's 20 of March 1993 and that's the day before the exchange of C 07. Madam Abata [phoen] of the UNHCR, a responsible high-ranking official, made similar dire predictions to the United Nations, and issued grave warnings about the imminent fate of Srebrenica. Dr. Mardel, a serious and committed WHO doctor, shared these concerns. So did Tony Birtley, so did Colonel Dudley. So did everyone who saw the situation, and that was why it was made into a safe area although that too in the end failed to save the people of Srebrenica. So as Colonel Tucker said, Oric had a job to do: "He had far more dangerous and worrisome issues on his mind than -- I do not wish to sound callous but [unintelligible] prisoners. There was much, much more on his mind than prisoners." Now, Naser Oric had a job to do in March 1993 when the most ferocious Serb offence such was under way and during which he himself was severely injured in the Achilles tendon as documentary evidence and the evidence of Meholjic plainly shows. And he had to job to do before that, throughout 1992, when the Serbs were daily attacking Potocari. That was the accused's area. It was where the hardest fighting was occurring and where he was needed the most. And that's where he was, not visiting the SUP every day in late September to mid-October, as the Prosecution contends, or as their witness Mr. Zikic contends. The law on command responsibility and the case law of this Tribunal recognises the vital importance of what was going on in the theatre of war at the relevant time. Your Honours will recognise that the accused was needed at the front lines in 1992 and 1993, that it was a life-or-death struggle not just for him but for the thousands in Srebrenica, and that the responsibility for the prison and prisoners fell on the shoulders of the civilian authorities in the town. And it's worth remembering that's where the detention facilities were, in the town, the SUP, the civilian police building, and the building which was located right behind the seat of the War Presidency. What happened in the town of Srebrenica was the War Presidency's responsibility. It had responsibility for law and order, and people like Bogilovic, Nurif Jusufovic, Mirzet Halilovic, Hajrudin Avdic, were all in the town, in the municipality building; they were not at the front lines apart from Mirzet Halilovic when he was removed from his post and then had to go to the front lines and indeed was killed in Skelani. It was Nurif Jusufovic, the civilian police chief, who dealt with detainees, who with Zele, the one-armed civilian policeman, that took young Branko -- my apologies, it was Zele who took young Branko Mitrovic from the SUP, and Avdic, ultimately, the president of the War Presidency, who were responsible for Serb detainees, and as documents show, and was shown by them refurbishing the building, the second location, and getting blankets for the detainees. That's a very direct, immediate, tangible piece of evidence that you can see in that regard, that actually Avdic and these others were involved in refurbishing the very premises where the Serb detainees were held. Clearly, this was their responsibility and not that of the accused. Your Honours, in the chaotic and improvised situation such as existed in Srebrenica, to determine effective control, not what is on paper but effective control, it's essential to have witness testimony regarding who reported to whom, and who controlled whom. Now, not a single witness said that Mirzet Halilovic delivered reports from the military police to the accused. On the contrary, Prosecution witnesses Meholjic and Bogilovic, and Defence witnesses Sacirovic and Djilovic, testified clearly, categorically, unambiguously, and on the basis of firsthand experience, that Halilovic reported to Bogilovic and to Avdic. They saw him bring his reports. And that's the only concrete evidence that you have on this matter. They and Prosecution witnesses testified that Halilovic was appointed by the War Presidency and dismissed by the War Presidency, not by the accused. At least, at the very least, all of this raises a reasonable doubt that the accused had effective control over the military police. In fact, it does not merely raise a reasonable doubt; the true picture is very clear: Oric and the fighters were fighting on the front lines while the War Presidency ran the town through the civilian police, in which the so-called military police were incorporated. These police forces were based in the SUP, where prisoners were held, and which later spilled over into the building behind the municipal building. This is a picture which has not only been confirmed; it makes sense; if fits the facts best. Now, you'll recall Becir Bogilovic and his demeanour before this Court. Your Honour had to warn him several times not to be evasive. This is the man whom Sead Bekric testified shot a hat off his head, risking killing him, simply because it was a policeman's hat. He was the boss of Mirzet Halilovic, and he in turn reported to the War Presidency. Now, Your Honours, unlike the Prosecution, we don't pretend that the documentary and oral evidence is a seamless fabric which shows only one picture, the picture we have presented. In Srebrenica, there was chaos, then attempts to restore order, and then final chaos before the descent into the abyss. People tried to unite, they tried to create institutions, they tried to impose control where there was anarchy. And it's only natural that they tried. People were confused as to who should do what and who had what power. And as Prosecution witness Mujkanovic said - I believe we have a slide - "During the Srebrenica disaster or the downfall of Srebrenica in 1992 and 1993, neither the civilian bodies nor the military bodies were ever organised in a way that was prescribed by law. You did not know who was superior or who was subordinate to whom or what fell under the jurisdiction of the civilian bodies and of the army respectively. This was a scene of total chaos, where no one knew who they were responsible to and for what. It was unclear who was making the appointments, or who was being appointed, for that matter." Now, confusion as to the chain of command, particularly in relation to the military police, negates the concept of effective control, as Prosecution witness Hogic confirmed on the 12th of May 2005, at T8172 to T8174. If the military police even had two commands, the War Presidency and the staff, it could not function as a competent and responsible body according to the applicable rules and regulations. Now, in light of that, when Your Honours weigh two possible explanations of an event, applying, as it were, the scales of justice, we know that you'll place a gold ingot on the side of the accused, representing the presumption of innocence, because the scales of justice are not level. They are tipped in favour of the accused. And it's the genius of an enlightened criminal justice system that the accused is not presumed guilty, he does not have to prove beyond a reasonable doubt his innocence, and he does not have to endure trial by fire or water before he can be acquitted. It suffices that the Prosecution have not proved their case, and the Prosecution have not proved their case here in relation to any of the charges. Now, the matter is in Your Honours' hands, and you bear the fateful responsibility for deciding such important issues without fear or favour of the consequences or of how your judgement will be perceived one way or the other. As Your Honour said at one stage in this trial, you're not here to give out medals. Nor are you here to convict a person simply to appease others or to comfort the sense of victimhood on the part of certain individuals. And you will recall even that those individuals did not ask for justice to be done by treating the commander as a sacrificial lamb. As Mr. Radic, a man who suffered a great deal, said,"I would never have Mr. Naser Oric convicted if it were up to me. If it were up to me, I would set him free right now, and I would dearly like to see Kemo in Mr. Naser Oric's place. I was never for anything like that including Naser Oric. Naser Oric never caused me any harm." Yet Kemo walks free, untouched by any of this, as far as we know, not even and interviewed, as far as we can tell, and the Prosecution requests 18 years' imprisonment for Naser Oric on behalf of victims who would never ask for such punishment in their name. Now, Your Honour, I'm going to turn to some remarks on sentencing and so this would be an appropriate time for the pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. Before you do so, or before we have the break, for tomorrow please take note of the following, particularly the Prosecution. We still have some unfinished symphonies to deal with. One relates to Prosecution Exhibit P570, in relation to the 32 pages that I had suggested to you that you consider removing so that you avoid the problem that had been raised by the Defence. You haven't come back to us as yet. The other is in relation to Defence Exhibit D690. On the 10th of March of this year, upon the suggestion from the Defence of removing indicated pages from the book as Exhibit 691, restricting it only to the pages that were used with witnesses, you said, "I would just ask that I am going to consult with my colleagues in the very beginning of next week. The position right now that we would voice is we would want the other pages to remain in, but if we can reach another decision, we will certainly convey it to the Defence and to the Trial Chamber." We have not heard from you or from the Defence on this. I am informed, as in relation to P599, that a new translation has been provided, which I haven't seen. I think the translation was provided today. So if you have any comment on that, please come forward by not later than tomorrow. Then there is the Philipp von Recklinghausen Rule 92 bis statement. I found out that, for unknown reasons, we failed to give it an exhibit number. So I'm giving it an exhibit number, being D1024. All right. I think that's all I needed to tell you. In relation to P84.1 and P598.1, I think I have already made it clear that, for the time being, they are entered into the records, but, of course, we will decide whether they will stay or not in the course of the deliberations. But the other initial matters, please try to address at some point in time tomorrow. All right? Thank you. We'll have a -- Mr. Jones, I see that you have advanced considerably, and that you have only got sentencing left.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So do you require 25 minutes or 30 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: 30 minutes would be ample, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, the Prosecution did not state publicly at any time during its closing speech the sentence that they had requested for Naser Oric. So I've had to do it for them. The Prosecutor of this Tribunal, Carla Del Ponte requested 18 years imprisonment for our client. 18 years. Despite all the evidence of the appalling situation in Srebrenica, all of what Prosecution witnesses have said about the terrible responsibility that Naser Oric bore, even the sympathetic noises made by the investigators during the suspect interview about the difficulties faced by the accused, when it comes to sentencing, all that is forgotten. The Prosecution has apparently not a single shred of human sympathy for the accused's predicament in that period. In the final brief of the Prosecution, there is not one line, not an ounce of recognition, of anything which the Prosecution considers mitigating, just a cold-hearted demand for the most Draconian sentence. I trust that the world -- the world -- will judge the credibility of this Prosecutor, Ms. Carla Del Ponte, on this record, for asking for such a sentence in a case based on the facts and the evidence that we've all seen. Is this the face of compassionate criminal justice, the better hope -- sorry, the hope for a better future, for peace and reconciliation for the world, or is it a face in which the light of human kindness and empathy does not flicker, an organ wielding its enormous prosecutorial powers without a corresponding sense of responsibility? History will be the judge of that. The Prosecutor's recommendation of a sentence of 18 years bears no relation to justice or sentencing practice. The Prosecution wishes to punish the accused vindictively and cruelly simply for maintaining his innocence and for mounting a vigorous defence. This is a Prosecutor who recommended that Miroslav Deronjic receive ten years for a crime against humanity, for a crime against humanity in Glogova, in Bratunac municipality, in which more than 65 people were murdered and the whole village burned, including the mosque. And incidentally if you consult the indictment, you'll see Najdan Mladjenovic, whom my colleague mentioned yesterday, appearing in that indictment as a perpetrator of mass killings. It's yet again a reflection of this warped world in which we appear to live in this case in which the victims become -- the perpetrators become the victims. In fact, the burning of that village, that Muslim village of Glogova, is now blamed on the Accused in what's perhaps the ultimate irony. You'll see that on the slide, the Prosecution's final brief, page 300, Naser Oric is now accused of burning Glogova, a village burnt by Miroslav Deronjic or on his orders. Now, we are not saying that Deronjic deserved more or less than ten years' imprisonment. That's not a matter for us. But according to the Prosecution Deronjic was responsible for the murders of tens of people, and yet the Prosecution asked only for ten years. In this case, the Accused is charged with six murders and cruel treatment and wanton destruction. One would understand from this that Serb property is more important than Muslim lives. If the Prosecution's sentencing policy were based on a concern for victims, you would never see such a disparity. Or is the Prosecution more concerned with securing cooperation than with the suffering of victims? The Prosecution will respond that in cases like Deronjic, the Accused cooperated. Some defendants no doubt have a stronger incentive than others to cut deals to try and reduce their sentence. It is not the most principled reason for leniency. But even so, in most jurisdictions a guilty plea and cooperation will reduce a sentence somewhat, but not to such an absurd disparity where the Prosecution considers that this accused deserves nearly twice the imprisonment that they recommended for Miroslav Deronjic. Moreover, as we pointed out in our response to the Prosecution's final brief, the factual basis for the Prosecution's recommendation is full of completely untrue statements. I would point something out to Your Honour which is that we pointed out these misstatements in the final brief on which the Prosecution based their recommendation. Now, did the Prosecution look at the position and consider and realise that they had got that wrong and then revise the sentence they requested as, of course, one would expect them to do when they see that their basis was mistaken? No, the sentence remains the same. What can one conclude from that? Well, that in fact the sentence which the Prosecution requests isn't based on cooperation or non-cooperation. It's not based on facts or evidence. It's simply a retributive -- a demand for retribution for an accused, as I say, simply maintaining his innocence. The Prosecution falsely states that the accused "has not cooperated with the Prosecution at any stage of the proceedings." Yet the Accused's interview at length by the Prosecution was interviewed at length by the Prosecution and volunteered to surrender if indicted which the Prosecution denied him the opportunity to do. And during the suspect interview, provided samples of his signature and we agreed the evidence of Tedder and Kelly [phoen], P380 and P382, which enabled forensics to go ahead. The Prosecution falsely states that the accused "has not conceded one aspect of the case. He has not agreed to any evidence." As I say we agreed the evidence of Tedder and Kelly. We conceded 43 agreed facts. That's P562. Now, those following this case will realise that there is nothing to be gained by any cooperation with the Prosecution unless it ends in a guilty plea. The Prosecution will deny that any cooperation was received even when it was. They will deny that admissions were made so there is no point in making them. Their approach will only discourage any form of cooperation. Throughout this case, we as Defence counsel have done all we could to expedite the proceedings and to cooperate with our professional colleagues. We have not been repaid in kind. For the Prosecution it seems the only good accused is an accused who pleads guilty and cooperates with their office. They would use the sentencing power as an arbitrary instrument of retribution for those who dare to proclaim their innocence and make life inconvenient for their office. Your Honours must not be a party to this cynical practice. Worse still is what this means for Srebrenica. The Prosecution has suggested that the Defence witnesses from Srebrenica should not be believed because they are involved in the events there, they are victims of the events there. The Prosecution should then immediately abandon all its Prosecutions of Serbs for the July 1995 genocide since it will have to rely on such inherently suspect witnesses. Maybe the witnesses, when they learn of how poorly they are regarded by this Prosecutor, will decide not to testify on behalf of the Prosecution any way. The Prosecution's case has been about a systematic rewriting of the story of Srebrenica. So Srebrenica was betrayed in 1995, it is now betrayed a second time by this Prosecution. We find in the Prosecution's final brief sentences such as the following: "During the period May 1992 to February 1993, Muslim armed units engaged in various military operations against the Army" -- capital A -- "of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." The picture is clear from that isn't it? For the Prosecution the legitimate army and state was the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina whose army was attacked by rogue Muslim units. One would never guess from this that these Muslim units were loyal to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a state recognised by the United Nations and the European Union. And then the Prosecution characterises the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina in this way: "In essence, the armed conflict involved the most fundamental and salient issues in warfare, the mutually competing interests of two states in securing their territorial integrity. Now it is indeed sad that Slobodan Milosevic did not live to see these words written by the Prosecution as he would find in them affirmation that Serbia and Montenegro had an interest, a mutually competing interest to annex territory of the neighbouring state in breach of the UN charter in order to "secure its territorial integrity," and apparently this interest is no worse than Bosnia-Herzegovina's interest in remaining an integral state. These and countless examples from this trial are symptomatic of the moral equivalents that we warned would cast its shadow over the trial. It need not have been this way. The Prosecution did not need to defend Serbia and the Bosnian Serb army to maintain its case. And that it does so, this is why I mention it, it's a potent warning that those who say these trials are free of politics are not correct. A political agenda in this trial does indeed -- excuse me, a political agenda does indeed hang over this trial to lay the blame for the 1995 genocide at the doorstep of the Muslims. And history will deliver its own verdict on that agenda. Why do we insist on this point? Look at what the Prosecution says at the end of its final brief: The accused "has attempted to provide an utterly false picture," an utterly false picture, they say, "of the command structure he presided over." And then they go on to say that therefore he is deserving of a severe sentence. Now it's no accident that that statement is placed right at the end of the brief for maximum impact. But of all the statements in this trial this is the most extraordinary. Let us first recall that the accused never gave evidence so the presentation must therefore apply to the testimony of Defence witnesses who came here and gave their evidence under oath and not one of whom was challenged by the Prosecution as being untruthful when he gave that evidence. The Prosecution called witness after witness to testify, and those witnesses painted exactly the same picture of events in Srebrenica as Defence witnesses did. Mujkanovic, Meholjic, Bogilovic, Becirovic, Omerovic, Delic, their own international witnesses testified to the same effect. So did Ambassador Arria, the former ambassador of Venezuela who led a Security Council mission to Srebrenica. So Drs. Mardell [phoen] and Dachy said honourably in Srebrenica on the behalf of extremely eminent medical foundations. The same picture was painted by US Colonel Rex Dudley an American army officer, and Canadian Captain McDonald, a trained UN observer. Tony Birtley who won awards for his coverage of events in Srebrenica painted the same picture. Yet it follows from what the Prosecution says here that all these witnesses should be brought back and prosecuted for false testimony. They should be sentenced to stiff sentences for presenting such a grievously false picture of events in Srebrenica. The books of Fink and Hollingworth should be withdrawn from bookstores since they are also so full of untruths. It's nonsense, Your Honour. Those witnesses, Prosecution and Defence, have told it like it was. So why is the Prosecution so full of vitriol against the Accused? Well the answer is they could not bend him to their will so they wish to crush him. You may be familiar with Rodin's famous sculpture, the Burghers of Calais. Like the Burghers of Calais, a Rodin sculpture, Naser Oric is to be punished severely simply for resisting their will. And why is the Prosecution so furious about the picture presented of the chaos in Srebrenica and of the lack of structure in the armed forces? Why is it such a heresy to tell the truth about Srebrenica? Because the world failed Srebrenica, the UN, the Dutch, the west, everyone who could have stepped in to save the people and did not, and the accused, as a symbol of Srebrenica's resistance is an inconvenient reminder of that fact. Which is what makes his conviction so convenient to so many. And, Your Honours, I say all of this once more simply so that you banish all of it from your minds and simply judge the accused on the facts because those facts argue more eloquently for his acquittal than any speech of mine could do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. I take it there is nothing else on the agenda today. Tomorrow we will be sitting in the afternoon. I'll be sitting in the morning at 8.00 and later but then we'll meet in this case at 2.15. And please try to address all the issues that I raised with you, particularly Prosecution -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I discussed with learned counsel during the break, and we would both like to put forward if there are any issues in particular that the Trial Chamber would have us both address tomorrow, if you want to tell us those issues today or indicate what would be specific areas, we would be more than willing to try and therefore tailor more specific questions -- answers to your questions or inquiries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Brydensholt is going to give you an indication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Well, even if I don't have the transcript so I can't show the exact page, but I noticed that Ms. Richardson mentioned that your submission is that it was the military police which guarded or at least persons even if they were in civil clothes, guarded the prisoners in both places. I would like you to explain on what ground you maintain that. And on the same line, I would ask the Defence to make it clear to me whether your submission that it was the military police which guarded the prisoners in both places, or it wasn't. It has not become quite clear to me what your position is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge Brydensholt. Judge Eser?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Perhaps I may address one issue. But I have further questions I would like to go over the transcript before I put them tomorrow. At least there is one issue which has also been addressed by the Defence. And it concerns the question of responsibility of soldier or guards with regard to actions by civilians, opportunistic visitors as they have been called, in the final brief of the Prosecution there are some references to acts committed by civilians in paragraphs 234 and the following, but if you go to the -- for instance to the villages, wanton destruction and so on, most of the time, for instance, if you go to paragraph 577, the Prosecution would only speak of the people who demonstrate the following: "Soldiers under the command of the accused unlawfully burned houses. There is no reference at all that civilians may have done it. And the same is true with regard to the other villages. For instance I think it's paragraph 504, 650, 698, 737, 744, that the Prosecution would only speak of soldiers and not mention at all any aiding and abetting to acts committed by civilians. So this is one point which I would like to hear a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As far as I am concerned, I think more or less I gave you some indications yesterday. I'll probably have a few more questions, but I would like to go through my notes first. But they shouldn't be that problematic to answer. One definitely relates to the legal position in relation to the signatures examined by Professor Bilic, that neither Dr. Kerzan nor Dr. Fagel or Dr. Koeijer examined, and I would like to know your approach on this or your position on this, particularly since the onus of proving the authenticity of the documents that you have tendered will always rest with you, and the Defence have got no obligation to prove that any of the documents that you have tendered is not authentic. The Prosecution -- the Defence may embark on a task of inserting in the proceedings an element of doubt, and whatever the Defence tries to achieve by that can be achieved on a balance of probabilities' basis. So at this point in time, forgetting for a moment your submission that Professor Bilic is not reliable by -- independent of that submission and without prejudice to it, what is the legal position that emerges from the fact that there is a report by one of the experts, a Defence expert, that throws doubt on a number of documents that have not been examined by any other expert, neither yours nor ours. That's one of the aspects I would like you to deal with tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Perhaps in addition to what I already indicated, in the meantime I found out that the question of responsibility, command responsibility, for aiding and abetting by subordinates with regard to crimes committed by civilians, this issue was mentioned in the closing arguments by Mr. Di Fazio. I think it was on pages 12 following, where he speaks of soldiers aiding and abetting to crimes by civilians. Mrs. Sellers with talk of military police and soldiers, and Ms. Richardson would only speak of military police. So it should be clarified to what persons command responsibility may be concerned with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And lastly, maybe one point that I would address to you. I mean, for example, there are two documents, Defence -- sorry, excuse me, Prosecution exhibits, falling in the category that you attack as not having been put to any witness. I refer you to P253 and P443. It seems to me that you make use of them yourselves in your final brief. So what -- does that change anything from your previous submissions on this category of documents? Also, you make ample use in your final brief of P84, for example, while you attack it at the same time. And also, the field, what you call, or meadow or diary or whatever, again you attack it in more ways than one but you also make use of it, and you make use of it -- when I say you, I might mean either of you, made use of it even in the course of today. So -- and there are other documents from the Sokolac collection that -- and other documents from Republika Srpska that you also referred to and make use of, not just refer to in the Defence final brief. I would like you to address that tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I followed that fully, Your Honour. I was going to give a quick answer which is that often if it's a case if it's authentic then other consequences follow but not that we're relying on the document itself. But I can't have any more detailed answer. May I mention two housekeeping matters for tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One is that since the Prosecution, of course, can prepare for tomorrow in light of what we've been saying over the last two days, we are not in a like position. So I've asked my learned friends if they intend to rely on any legal authority tomorrow. If they could let us know beforehand so that we are in a position to respond to that. That's one matter. The other matter is, I think we are all keen to finish, certainly the parties and possibly the Bench as well, but to finish tomorrow if possible and to the extent that we'd even be prepared to accept or to impose on ourselves a sort of time limit so that we can be -- safely be away. Part of that, I suppose, depends on how long Your Honours would also like to allocate. But for our part we would be happy to say each side has one hour or half an hour, but just so we can be sure that we finish because some of us have travel plans. Not us. Not on this side, I should say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start with the Prosecution. Would one hour be sufficient for you?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that we would aim for one hour, maximum. If it could be less we will certainly abide by the less-than-one-hour timetable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But in that case, you wouldn't entrust the task to Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't divulge the Prosecutor's work product on those issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we better play it on the safe side. We'll say one hour each. If you need less, then obviously you cut it short without corresponding duty on the other side to cut it short too. So let's say you have got a maximum of one hour each, with our indulgence should you require more. But let's say one hour tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I think we would even be prepared to say that we will take only as long as the Prosecution does so that it's not a question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can't force you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's simply to indicate that we wouldn't be proposing to prepare a one-hour presentation tomorrow. We will be responding to what the Prosecution says and so we may be only five or ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO: Just to make sure that things move smoothly tomorrow, the Prosecution is in the process of preparing a spread sheet that's going to show where some of the documents that we have used as Prosecution exhibits come from. In other words, the collection they come from. The various sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have done that exercise already myself so -- MR. DI FAZIO: Would you be served if we gave you that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, of course, of course. First of all, I will find out how many mistakes I have made. MR. DI FAZIO: What I'll do is get it done and send it to the Defence today and -- excuse me. That can be done. And we'll rely on that, perhaps hand it up tomorrow and Your Honours can have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Great. I thank you so much. So, please God, tomorrow afternoon, 2.15, and we'll try to finish the sitting as soon as possible. I thank you.
